questions.from: Three modules back — The Judgement You Can't Remove
questions.prompt: Why does automation bias make a highly accurate system more dangerous in some ways, not less?

options.label: Higher accuracy makes reviewers stop checking carefully, because the system is usually right
Accuracy has no relationship to automation bias
Higher accuracy always eliminates the need for review entirely

questions.explanation: A reviewer who's learned a system is usually right tends to stop actually checking it, which is exactly what lets the rare wrong decision through unreviewed — the mechanism behind that module's title.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: Drawing the pipeline before choosing anything
description: Sequencing questions — what happens before what, where a human sits, what a step actually needs from the one before it — only surface once the pipeline is drawn, and they're expensive to discover after tools are already chosen.

learningObjectives.text: Draw a proposed automation as a sequence of discrete steps with explicit inputs and outputs before selecting any tool
Identify sequencing questions a pipeline diagram surfaces that a tool-first approach misses

contentSections.body: Fennimore Freight Brokers moves about ninety load tenders a week — shippers emailing a PDF or spreadsheet naming a shipment, a pickup window, and a rate. The operations director, energized after last module's tool evaluation, says: "let's just start building the extraction bot." Nobody has yet drawn what actually has to happen to a tender between arriving in an inbox and appearing, correctly, in Fennimore's dispatch system — and that gap is where the real design decisions live.

A pipeline is a sequence of discrete steps, each with something specific it receives and something specific it hands to the next step. Drawing it — on paper, in a diagram tool, it doesn't matter which — before choosing any tool forces answers to questions a tool-first approach skips past:

Which step happens before which? Does validation happen before or after a human reviews an ambiguous tender, or after? Where does a person actually sit in the sequence — reviewing everything, reviewing only flagged items, or not at all until something goes wrong? What does each step actually need from the step before it, in a form it can use — not just "the tender," but which specific fields, in which format?

None of these are tool questions. They're sequencing and contract questions, and getting them wrong doesn't show up as a bug in any one tool — it shows up as two correctly-functioning tools that don't fit together, discovered only once both are already built.

contentSections.question: Fennimore's load-tender process, undrawn, in the operations director's head, mixes several distinct things together. Put these into the order they'd appear as separate boxes on an actual pipeline diagram.
steps: Tender arrives by email as a PDF or spreadsheet attachment
Fields (shipper, pickup window, rate, equipment type) are extracted from the document
Extracted fields are checked against required-field rules and flagged if anything's missing or implausible
A dispatcher reviews any flagged tender before it proceeds
The tender is written into Fennimore's dispatch system as a bookable load
contentSections.explanation: Each of these is a genuinely separate step with its own input and output, even though "process the tender" describes all five in one breath. Extraction has to happen before validation, because you can't check fields that haven't been pulled out yet. Validation has to happen before the dispatcher review, because the whole point of the review step is looking at what validation flagged — reviewing before validation would mean reviewing everything, which defeats the purpose of having a validation step at all. And writing to the dispatch system comes last, because it's the step that makes the tender real and bookable — nothing before it should have effects outside the pipeline itself.

contentSections.code: Fennimore's actual first attempt, built without a diagram: the extraction bot reads a tender and immediately writes whatever it finds straight into the dispatch system, tagged 'needs review.' A dispatcher is supposed to check the 'needs review' queue at some point before the load ships.
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this design, visible only once you draw where the review step actually sits?

options.label: The tender becomes a real, bookable load in the dispatch system before anyone has reviewed it — the review happens after the step that was supposed to gate it, not before
Extraction bots are inherently unreliable and shouldn't be used at all
Dispatchers should never review tenders, since the whole point is to remove manual work

feedback.review-after-effect: Correct. Writing to the dispatch system is the step that makes a tender real and actionable — a driver could be dispatched against it. Tagging it 'needs review' after that write has already happened means the review is checking something that can already have consequences, not gating whether those consequences happen. Drawing the pipeline out would have shown the write-step happening before the review-step, when the intent was the reverse.
feedback.unreliable: The flaw isn't about extraction accuracy at all — it's about where the human check sits relative to the step that has real-world effects. Even a perfectly accurate extraction step would have this same sequencing problem.
feedback.no-review: The lesson isn't that dispatchers shouldn't review — reasonable human review is exactly what's missing effectively here. The flaw is that the review is positioned after the consequential step instead of before it.

contentSections.flawExplanation: "Needs review" as a tag on an already-written record isn't a gate — it's a note. A gate stops something from happening until a condition is met; a tag just labels something that's already happened. This is exactly the kind of ordering mistake that a pipeline diagram, drawn before any tool is chosen, would have surfaced by forcing the question "does the write happen before or after the review?" in plain sight.

contentSections.body: Draw the pipeline — the actual sequence of steps, what gates what, where a person sits — before choosing a single tool. Sequencing mistakes don't show up as bugs in a tool; they show up as two working tools that don't fit together.

title: What each step receives and guarantees
description: Two steps built by two different people fail to connect not because either one is broken, but because neither one wrote down exactly what it receives and exactly what it promises to hand off — a step contract.

learningObjectives.text: Write an explicit contract for a pipeline step: its required inputs, its guaranteed outputs, and what success and failure mean for it
Diagnose a pipeline break caused by mismatched assumptions between two adjacent steps

contentSections.title: Two working steps that don't connect

contentSections.body: At Fennimore, one engineer builds the extraction step and outputs a field called `rate`. A different engineer, working from the same pipeline diagram a week later, builds the validation step expecting a field called `totalRate`. Both steps work perfectly on their own. Nothing connects them, and the failure doesn't look like a bug — it looks like validation silently treating every tender as missing its rate, because the field it's looking for was never named `rate` to begin with.

A pipeline diagram shows the sequence; it doesn't specify what actually passes between steps. That's a **step contract** — three things, written down, for every step: what it requires as input (field names, types, whether each is required or optional), what it guarantees as output (same, for what it hands the next step), and what counts as success versus failure for this specific step, not the pipeline as a whole.

The Fennimore break wasn't a coding error in either step — both worked exactly as their own author intended. It was a missing contract: nobody wrote down, in a place both engineers could check against, that the field is called `rate` and is a number in cents, not a formatted currency string. A contract turns an implicit assumption held in one person's head into something checkable by whoever builds the next step, or checks it later.

contentSections.problem: Write the contract for Fennimore's extraction step: input is a raw email attachment (PDF or spreadsheet); output needs to feed the validation step.

steps.label: Input requirement
steps.work: One attachment, either PDF or XLSX, under 10MB, containing a single load tender (not a batch of several tenders in one file).
steps.why: Stating the format, size limit, and 'single tender per file' assumption explicitly is what lets validation's author know exactly what kind of input extraction is guaranteed to have processed — and what it wasn't built to handle, like a multi-tender batch file.

steps.label: Output guarantee
steps.work: A record with fields: shipper_name (string), pickup_window_start (ISO 8601 datetime), pickup_window_end (ISO 8601 datetime), rate_cents (integer), equipment_type (string, one of a fixed list). Any field extraction couldn't find is explicitly null, never omitted from the record.
steps.why: Naming exact field names and types is what prevents the rate/totalRate mismatch. 'Explicitly null, never omitted' matters specifically: a missing key and a null value look identical to a careless reader but mean different things to code checking for a field's presence.

steps.label: Success/failure definition for this step
steps.work: Success: a record was produced, regardless of how many fields are null. Failure: the attachment couldn't be opened or parsed at all (corrupt file, unsupported format).
steps.why: This is the distinction that matters most for the next lesson on partial failure — a tender with three null fields is a success for extraction (it produced a record; validation's job is to catch the nulls), while an unopenable file is a genuine extraction failure that needs a different response.

faded.problem: Second case, same procedure. Write the contract for Fennimore's validation step: input is the extraction step's output record; its job is to check required fields and flag anything missing or implausible for dispatcher review.

blanks.prompt: What's the input requirement, stated precisely?
blanks.answer: A record matching extraction's exact output schema: shipper_name, pickup_window_start, pickup_window_end, rate_cents, equipment_type, with nulls explicit where extraction couldn't find a value
accept: the extraction record with its five named fields, nulls allowed but explicit
blanks.why: Validation's input requirement is just extraction's output guarantee, restated from the receiving side — this is what makes the contract a genuine handoff rather than two separate documents that happen to be adjacent.

blanks.prompt: What's the output guarantee — what does validation hand to the dispatcher-review step?
blanks.answer: The same record, plus a flags field listing which required fields are null or implausible, plus a boolean needsReview
accept: the record with an added list of problems found and a review flag
blanks.why: Validation doesn't just pass or fail a tender wholesale — its actual job is to produce a specific, checkable list of what's wrong, which is what makes the dispatcher's review step fast rather than a re-check of everything from scratch.

blanks.prompt: What counts as success versus failure for validation specifically?
blanks.answer: Success: validation ran and produced a flags list, even if the list is long. Failure: validation couldn't process the record at all, e.g. a field type it wasn't built to handle
accept: success is producing a flags list regardless of length; failure is validation itself crashing on the input
blanks.why: Same distinction as extraction: a tender with five flagged problems is validation working correctly, not validation failing — conflating 'found a lot of issues' with 'the step failed' is a common contract-writing mistake that hides real step failures inside a pile of normal flagged tenders.

faded.procedure: For every step: state the input precisely enough that the previous step's author and this step's author agree on it without a conversation, state the output precisely enough that the next step's author can build against it sight unseen, and separate 'this step found a problem with the data' from 'this step itself failed to run' — those are different failure classes with different responses.

contentSections.scenario: You're reviewing a colleague's draft contract for Fennimore's dispatch-write step (the last step, which books the load). Some parts of the draft genuinely belong in a step contract. Others are true statements about the step that don't belong in a contract meant for the next builder to work from.
contentSections.question: Select every item that belongs in the step contract itself.

items.label: Which fields are required (non-null) before this step will attempt to write a booking, and which are optional
What counts as failure for this step specifically — e.g. the dispatch system's API rejecting the write, distinct from a field being missing
What this step returns on success — a booking ID that downstream monitoring can reference
Which engineer originally built this step
How many times a day this step typically runs
That the dispatch system Fennimore uses is called TMSPro

explanation.required-fields: Applicable. This is the input half of the contract — exactly what the previous step (validation) must guarantee before this step can safely run.
explanation.write-failure-def: Applicable. Distinguishing 'the data was bad' from 'the write itself failed' is exactly the success/failure precision the worked example just walked through, applied to this step.
explanation.output-record-id: Applicable. This is the output guarantee — what a monitoring system or a human checking on a specific tender can expect to reference afterward.
explanation.built-by: Not applicable. Who built it is useful for finding someone to ask a question, but it isn't part of what the step receives, guarantees, or means by success and failure — it doesn't help the next builder build against this step.
explanation.how-often-runs: Not applicable to the contract itself — this is an operational fact about the pipeline's traffic, not a specification of the step's behavior. It might belong in a monitoring plan, not here.
explanation.dispatch-system-name: Not applicable as contract content, though it's a fact someone needs somewhere. A contract specifies behavior — inputs, outputs, success/failure — not which vendor product happens to sit behind the step today.

contentSections.synthesis: The three that belong are all specifications of behavior: what's required in, what's guaranteed out, and what success and failure mean. The three that don't belong are all true, useful facts about the step that live somewhere else — a team roster, a monitoring dashboard, a systems inventory — but would clutter a contract meant to let someone build the next step without a conversation.

contentSections.body: A pipeline diagram shows the sequence; a step contract specifies what actually passes between two steps — required inputs, guaranteed outputs, and what success and failure mean for that step specifically. Two working steps still fail to connect without one.

title: Queues, batches and things that run overnight
description: Load tenders don't arrive evenly — they arrive in a burst around 4pm as shippers close out their day, and a pipeline built to process one tender at a time backs up exactly when it matters most.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize when a pipeline needs a queue or batch design rather than one-at-a-time synchronous processing
Identify what an overnight batch job needs beyond correct logic — idempotency and monitoring — to run unattended safely

contentSections.body: Fennimore's load tenders don't arrive evenly across the day — they cluster hard around 4pm, as shippers finalize the next day's shipments before closing out. A pipeline built and tested processing one tender at a time, synchronously, handles the quiet morning hours fine and then falls behind every single afternoon, with tenders piling up in an inbox nobody's watching in real time until a dispatcher notices at 5:30 that nothing's moved in an hour.

One-at-a-time synchronous processing — read a tender, fully process it, then read the next — is the simplest design and the one that breaks first under a real arrival pattern. Two fixes, often used together:

**A queue.** Instead of processing immediately on arrival, a tender is dropped into a queue the moment it arrives, and a worker (or several, running in parallel) pulls from the queue as fast as it can. This decouples arrival rate from processing rate — a burst just makes the queue longer for a while, instead of blocking anything.

**Batching.** Some steps are more efficient run over many items at once than one at a time — particularly if there's a fixed per-call cost or setup, and rather than triggered on each new arrival, they run on a schedule, e.g. "process everything that's arrived since the last run, every 15 minutes" or, for lower-urgency work, "once, overnight."

An overnight batch job specifically needs two properties correct logic alone doesn't give you: **idempotency** — running it twice on the same data (because it crashed halfway and got restarted) must not produce duplicate bookings — and **monitoring that doesn't require a person watching** — because by definition nobody's awake to notice a 2am failure until morning, so the job needs to leave a clear, checkable record of what it did and didn't process.

contentSections.title: What makes an overnight job safe to run unattended

contentSections.scenario: Fennimore's overnight batch job processes the day's remaining tenders at 2am. One night, the job crashes at item 40 of 70 due to an unrelated network blip, and the scheduler automatically retries the whole job from the top an hour later. The next morning, dispatchers find the first 40 tenders booked twice, as duplicate loads in the dispatch system.
contentSections.question: What's the underlying design gap that turned a routine crash-and-retry into duplicate bookings?

options.label: The job wasn't idempotent — re-running it on tenders it had already booked created a second booking instead of recognizing they were already done
The network blip itself is the root cause and the only real fix is more reliable infrastructure
The job should never have been scheduled to run automatically overnight at all

feedback.not-idempotent: Correct. A network blip causing one crash is a normal, expected event that any overnight job design has to tolerate — the actual gap is that the job had no way to recognize "I already booked this tender" before booking it again. An idempotent version would check for an existing booking (or use a stable identifier the dispatch system itself would reject as a duplicate) before writing, so a retry from the top is safe by design rather than by luck.
feedback.network-cause: Infrastructure will always occasionally blip — that's close to a given, not a fixable root cause. Treating it as the thing to fix misses that the job's response to a routine failure (an unsafe retry) is the actual design gap, and a more reliable network wouldn't be a fix, just a lower-frequency version of the same latent problem.
feedback.no-overnight: The problem isn't running overnight — overnight batching is a reasonable design choice for lower-urgency backlog work. The problem is that this particular overnight job wasn't built to survive its own restart safely, which is fixable without abandoning the overnight approach.

contentSections.mechanism: An overnight job runs unattended by definition, which means crashes and restarts have to be assumed, not treated as exceptional. Idempotency — designing a step so running it twice on the same input has the same effect as running it once — is what makes an automatic retry safe instead of dangerous, and it has to be designed in deliberately; it doesn't happen by default.

contentSections.body: Match the design to the arrival pattern — a queue absorbs a burst instead of blocking on it. And any job meant to run unattended overnight needs to survive its own crash and restart without creating duplicates, plus a record a human can check in the morning without having watched it run.

title: What happens to an item that fails halfway
description: A tender that gets partway through the pipeline and then fails needs somewhere specific to go and someone specific responsible for it — 'stuck in processing with no worklist' is not a failure state, it's the absence of one.

learningObjectives.text: Design a pipeline's partial-failure handling — where a half-processed item goes and who owns resolving it
Distinguish a retryable failure from one that needs a person, and route each differently

contentSections.body: A Fennimore load tender makes it through extraction cleanly, then fails validation — the pickup window field extraction found doesn't parse as a valid date, because the shipper wrote it as "early next wk" instead of a date. The pipeline has no defined behavior for this. The tender sits in a database row with a status column that still says "processing," indistinguishable from a tender that's simply mid-flight and about to succeed. Nobody built a place to look for tenders like this, so nobody looks, until a shipper calls asking why their load never got booked.

"What happens when a step fails" needs an actual designed answer, not a default of "the pipeline stops advancing that item and nothing else happens." Three things a robust design needs:

**A distinct failed state, not a stuck 'processing' one.** An item that failed validation should be visibly, queryably different from one that's simply still in flight — a status like `needs_human_review` or `failed_validation`, not a timestamp quietly getting older.

**A retry-vs-escalate decision, made explicitly per failure type.** Some failures are transient and safe to retry automatically (a momentary API timeout). Others are permanent without a human decision (an ambiguous date string a model can't confidently parse) — retrying those just wastes a retry budget and delays the item further; they need to route straight to a person.

**An owner and a worklist.** Somewhere a person can actually see every item currently in a failed state, ideally with what specifically failed, so "I'll fix it when a shipper calls" isn't the de facto process. Fennimore's original design had none of these — the failure was invisible by construction, not by bad luck.

contentSections.code: Fennimore's revised design, after the "early next wk" incident: any tender that fails validation gets automatically retried by re-running the entire pipeline from extraction, up to 5 times, with no change to the input and no human notified.
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this fix?

options.label: Retrying a permanent, non-transient failure (an unparseable date the shipper actually wrote ambiguously) five times with unchanged input will fail identically five times, and still ends with no human ever notified
Five retries is too many — it should retry only once before giving up
Retrying from extraction instead of from validation wastes processing time

feedback.retry-wont-help: Correct. This failure isn't transient — the shipper's ambiguous date string doesn't change between attempt 1 and attempt 5, so all five attempts fail the same way, and the fix still ends exactly where the original problem was: nobody notified, the tender stuck, just now with five wasted attempts behind it instead of zero.
feedback.retry-count: The number of retries isn't the core issue — even one retry, or fifty, produces the same non-result on a non-transient failure. The flaw is retrying at all without distinguishing failure types, not the specific count chosen.
feedback.restart-point: Where the retry restarts from is a real inefficiency, but it's a minor one next to the bigger flaw — even restarting from validation instead of extraction, this design still never notifies a person and never escalates a failure a retry structurally cannot fix.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A retry is the right response to a failure that might succeed on a second attempt — a network blip, a momentary rate limit. It's the wrong response to a failure that's a property of the input itself, which will fail identically every time until something about the input or the process changes. The fix has to sort failures into these two categories and only automatically retry the first — the second needs a human, immediately, not after five identical wasted attempts.

contentSections.intro: Design Fennimore's actual failure-handling path for validation failures. Four fields.

fields.prompt: What should a tender's status become the moment validation fails, instead of staying 'processing'?

options.label: needs_human_review, distinct from every in-flight status
processing, unchanged, since it will eventually be retried

feedback.distinct-status: Right. A distinct, queryable status is what makes the failure visible to a worklist instead of indistinguishable from an item that's simply mid-flight.
feedback.unchanged: This reproduces the exact original problem — a tender that's failed and one that's about to succeed look identical, so nobody can build a worklist that finds the failed ones.

fields.prompt: For an unparseable date string like 'early next wk', what's the right automatic response?

options.label: route directly to a human, no automatic retry attempted
retry up to 5 times automatically before giving up

feedback.route-human: Right. This is a non-transient, input-level failure — the string doesn't change between attempts, so a retry can't help. The correct response is to spend zero retries and go straight to a person who can actually resolve the ambiguity.
feedback.auto-retry: This is the flawed fix from the spot-flaw — retrying a failure that's a property of the input just delays the eventual human involvement without ever helping.

fields.prompt: Who should be able to see every tender currently in needs_human_review, and how?

options.label: a named role (e.g. the on-shift dispatcher) with a queryable worklist view, not 'whoever picks up the phone when a shipper calls'
no one specifically — it surfaces naturally when a shipper eventually calls to ask

feedback.named-worklist: Right. A worklist a named role checks proactively is what turns a designed failure state into an actual working process, instead of a status field nobody looks at until a customer complains.
feedback.reactive: This is exactly the original failure mode, just with a properly labeled status field sitting unused. A correct status without anyone assigned to check it is only cosmetically better than no status at all.

fields.prompt: What should the worklist entry show the dispatcher, to make resolving it fast?

options.label: which specific field failed and why (e.g. 'pickup_window_start: could not parse \'early next wk\' as a date'), not just 'tender #4471 needs review'
just the tender ID, so the dispatcher re-reads the whole original document from scratch

feedback.specific-reason: Right. This mirrors the validation step's contract from the earlier lesson — its output was a specific flags list, not a bare pass/fail. Surfacing that specific reason is what makes the worklist entry fast to resolve instead of a fresh investigation every time.
feedback.id-only: This throws away exactly the diagnostic information validation already produced, forcing the dispatcher to redo the diagnosis validation already did — a worklist entry should be a head start, not a blank slate.

contentSections.synthesis: Together these four decisions turn "the pipeline stops and nothing happens" into an actual designed response: a visible status, a failure sorted correctly into retry-or-escalate, a person responsible for the worklist, and enough context on each entry that resolving it doesn't mean starting over.

contentSections.body: An item that fails halfway needs a distinct status, a retry-or-escalate decision made by failure type, and a named owner with a real worklist — not a timestamp that quietly stops updating.

title: Designing for the day the model is unavailable
description: A model API outage during Fennimore's 4pm burst isn't a hypothetical — vendor outages happen, and a pipeline with no fallback for one turns a vendor's bad afternoon into every tender that arrives during it silently piling up.

learningObjectives.text: Design a pipeline's fallback behavior for the specific case of the model provider being unavailable or degraded
Decide when a pipeline should queue-and-wait versus fail over to a manual path during a model outage

contentSections.body: Fennimore's extraction step calls a model API to read each tender's PDF. One Tuesday at 4:15pm — peak burst — the model provider has a twenty-minute outage. The pipeline was never designed with this in mind: every extraction call during those twenty minutes throws an error, the pipeline has no defined response beyond "log the error and move on," and thirty-one tenders effectively vanish from the process, sitting unextracted with no flag, no queue, and no one aware anything happened until a shipper calls the next morning.

A model provider being unavailable, rate-limited, or degraded isn't a hypothetical edge case — it's a routine operating condition for any pipeline that depends on one, and it needs a designed response, not "the call fails and whatever happens, happens."

Three pieces, matched to how urgent the step actually is: **retry with backoff** — for a step that isn't time-critical, waiting a few seconds and trying again (with increasing delay between attempts) absorbs most short outages without anyone noticing. **A circuit breaker** — after enough consecutive failures, stop hammering a clearly-down provider and switch state to "degraded," instead of queuing failed retries indefinitely. **A fallback path** — what actually happens to an item while the model is down: does it wait safely in a queue until the model's back (fine for non-urgent batch work), or does it need a manual path (a person types the fields in directly) because the business can't tolerate the delay?

The choice between "wait it out" and "fail over to manual" isn't generic — it depends on how urgent the specific step is and how long outages realistically last. Fennimore's extraction step, feeding an overnight batch, can usually just wait in a queue. A step feeding a same-day, time-sensitive commitment could not.

contentSections.title: The 4:15pm outage
contentSections.opening: The model provider's status page confirms a partial outage, no ETA given. Thirty-one tenders have arrived since 4:00pm and extraction is failing on all of them. You're on call.

respond.situation: You need to decide what happens to those thirty-one tenders right now.
respond.question: What's the right immediate move?

choices.label: Do nothing — the pipeline will eventually retry them once the provider recovers
choices.consequence: Without a circuit breaker or queue design, 'eventually retry' is not actually a behavior this pipeline has — it's an assumption about behavior nobody built. The thirty-one tenders are, right now, in the same invisible failed-and-unflagged state from the earlier lesson, and doing nothing leaves them there.

choices.label: Confirm the tenders are being held in a retry queue (not lost), and check whether extraction is urgent enough that waiting is actually acceptable here
choices.consequence: This is the right question to ask before deciding anything else — whether waiting is tolerable depends on how time-sensitive this specific step is, which for an overnight-batch-feeding step like Fennimore's extraction, it usually is.

choices.label: Immediately route all thirty-one to a person to key in manually, regardless of urgency
choices.consequence: This works, but it's expensive and premature for a twenty-minute outage on a step that isn't actually time-critical — jumping straight to the costliest fallback without checking whether the cheaper one (wait in queue) would have been fine wastes staff time on an outage that likely resolves on its own.

assess-urgency.situation: You confirm: the thirty-one tenders are safely queued (not lost), and extraction feeds an overnight batch that doesn't run until 2am — nine hours away. The provider's status page shows outages of this kind typically resolve within an hour.
assess-urgency.question: Given that, what's the right call?

choices.label: Let them wait in the queue with retry-and-backoff; nine hours of runway against a typically-under-an-hour outage means manual intervention isn't needed
choices.consequence: This matches the fallback to the actual urgency — a step fine with delay, facing a short outage, doesn't need the expensive fallback. If the outage were still ongoing close to the batch deadline, that would be the moment to reassess.

choices.label: Route them to manual entry anyway, just to be safe
choices.consequence: "Just to be safe" here means spending staff time that nine hours of slack against a typically-short outage didn't require — it's not wrong exactly, but it's over-engineering the response relative to the actual risk, and it's a habit that gets expensive if it becomes the default for every transient blip.

ignored.summary: The thirty-one tenders sit unextracted with no flag until someone notices tomorrow, functionally identical to the pipeline having no failure design at all — because for this outage, it didn't.
ignored.lesson: An assumption that the pipeline 'handles this somehow' isn't a design — if retry-and-queue behavior wasn't deliberately built, it doesn't exist just because it would be reasonable.

overreacted.summary: The tenders get processed, but at the cost of staff time spent hand-keying data that, as it turns out, would have cleared on its own within the hour — a fallback used when the cheaper option would have worked fine.
overreacted.lesson: Fail-over-to-manual is for when waiting genuinely isn't tolerable, not a reflexive first response to any outage — check urgency and expected outage length before paying the expensive fallback's cost.

overcautious.summary: Same outcome as overreacting, arrived at more carefully — the tenders get manually entered despite nine hours of slack that made it unnecessary, which is a smaller version of the same over-engineering.
overcautious.lesson: Checking urgency and still defaulting to the expensive fallback anyway wastes the analysis — the point of assessing urgency is to actually let it change the decision when the numbers say waiting is fine.

matched.summary: The tenders wait safely in the queue, extraction resumes automatically once the provider recovers within the hour, and the 2am batch runs with nine hours to spare. Nobody's afternoon was interrupted by an outage that resolved on its own.
matched.lesson: Matching the fallback to the step's actual urgency and the outage's likely duration is what keeps a routine vendor blip routine instead of turning it into either a silent data loss or an unnecessary all-hands response.

contentSections.body: A model outage is a routine operating condition, not an edge case — design retry-with-backoff, a circuit breaker, and a fallback path for it deliberately, and match the fallback's cost to how urgent the specific step actually is.

title: Lab — Specify a Full Pipeline Including Its Failure Paths
description: Take a real or realistic automation need, draw its pipeline, write a contract for every step, and specify what happens when a step fails halfway and when the model itself is unavailable.

learningObjectives.text: Specify a complete pipeline — steps, contracts, and failure paths — that an implementer could build from without asking a clarifying question

contentSections.body: Every design decision in this module got sharper the moment it was written down as a specific answer instead of an assumption. That's the lab: take one automation need — real or a concretely specified plausible one — and produce a full pipeline spec: the steps, what passes between them, and what happens when something fails.

contentSections.title: Your pipeline specification
contentSections.brief: Pick one specific automation need with at least three real processing steps — real or a concretely specified plausible one. You're going to draw its pipeline, write a contract for every step, and specify its failure paths, including a model-unavailable scenario, precisely enough that someone else could build it without asking you a clarifying question.
contentSections.deliverable: A pipeline spec: a diagram or ordered list of steps, a written contract (input, output, success/failure definition) for each step, a partial-failure design (status, retry-vs-escalate, owner), and a model-unavailable fallback design.

stages.title: Draw the pipeline
stages.instructions: Name the automation need concretely. List every real step in order, including where a human sits in the sequence. Check explicitly: does any step's output need to exist before another step could plausibly run? Fix the ordering before moving on.
stages.checkpoint: You have an ordered list of at least three steps, with the human-review step (if any) placed at a specific point, not left implicit.

stages.title: Write a contract for each step
stages.instructions: For every step: name its required and optional inputs with types, its guaranteed output fields, and what counts as success versus failure for that step specifically (not the whole pipeline).
stages.checkpoint: Every step has all three contract elements written down, and adjacent steps' input/output field names actually match each other.

stages.title: Design the partial-failure path
stages.instructions: Pick the step most likely to fail partway (a validation or extraction step is usually the candidate). Specify: what status a failed item gets, whether failures should auto-retry or route straight to a person, and who owns the resulting worklist.
stages.checkpoint: You have a named failure status distinct from any in-flight status, an explicit retry-vs-escalate rule, and a named worklist owner.

stages.title: Design the model-unavailable fallback
stages.instructions: For whichever step calls a model, specify what happens during an outage: does it wait in a queue (state why that's tolerable) or fail over to a manual path (state why waiting isn't)? Name the condition that would flip your answer.
stages.checkpoint: You have a stated fallback choice with a reason tied to the step's actual urgency, and a named condition that would change it.

rubric.criterion: The pipeline is a real ordered sequence, not a single bundled step
rubric.meets: At least three distinct steps are listed in an order that reflects genuine dependencies, with any human-review step placed at a specific point.

rubric.criterion: Every step has a complete contract
rubric.meets: Each step names its required/optional inputs, its output fields, and its own success/failure definition — and adjacent steps' fields actually match.

rubric.criterion: The partial-failure design is concrete
rubric.meets: A named failed status, an explicit retry-vs-escalate rule tied to failure type, and a named worklist owner are all present.

rubric.criterion: The model-unavailable fallback is justified, not assumed
rubric.meets: The wait-vs-manual choice is tied to the step's actual urgency and a realistic outage length, not asserted without reasoning.

rubric.criterion: An implementer could build from this without asking a clarifying question
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the need could start building any single step from its contract alone.

rubric.criterion: The spec names what would change the design
rubric.meets: At least one condition (a volume change, an urgency change) that would alter a specific decision is stated explicitly.

contentSections.body: A pipeline spec is only as useful as the decisions it actually forces someone to make on paper — sequencing, contracts, and failure paths written down are what let an implementer build without guessing.

questions.prompt: Fennimore's extraction step writes straight into the dispatch system tagged 'needs review,' with the review happening afterward. What's the actual flaw?

options.label: The tender becomes real and bookable before anyone reviews it — the review happens after the consequential step, not before
Extraction is too inaccurate to trust
Dispatchers shouldn't review tenders at all

questions.explanation: Drawing the pipeline would have shown the write-step (which has real effects) happening before the review-step, when the review was meant to gate it — a sequencing flaw, not an accuracy one.

questions.prompt: Two Fennimore engineers each build a working step, but validation expects a field called `totalRate` while extraction outputs `rate`. What's missing?

options.label: A step contract — a written specification of exactly what one step guarantees and what the next step requires
More extensive testing of the extraction step alone
A faster model for extraction

questions.explanation: Both steps worked correctly in isolation — the gap was a missing contract making the handoff between them explicit and checkable.

title: The prompt is the business logic now
description: A prompt edit that feels like a copy edit can silently change which claims get flagged urgent — the prompt is the thing making the decision, not documentation describing it, and it fails without ever looking broken.

learningObjectives.text: Recognize a prompt as an executable decision-making artifact rather than descriptive text
Distinguish a wording edit that changes model behavior from one that genuinely doesn't

contentSections.body:
Aldermere Property Claims runs a triage prompt that reads each inbound claim email and decides how urgently it needs a human. On a Friday afternoon, a junior teammate opens the shared doc holding the prompt and rewrites it to sound "friendlier" — swapping "the homeowner" for "the policyholder" throughout the instructions and examples. It reads like a tone fix. She ships it straight from the doc into the live config, the way everyone always has, and doesn't mention it in standup because it didn't feel like a change worth mentioning.

Over the weekend, urgency classification quietly gets worse for one specific group: claims from rental properties. Every few-shot example in the prompt that modeled a straightforward, clearly-urgent claim had used "the homeowner" as an incidental marker of a normal residential case. With that word gone, claims naming "the tenant" — which is most of Aldermere's rental-property water-damage claims — stop pattern-matching to the urgent examples as strongly. By Monday, fourteen weekend water-damage claims from rental units are sitting in the standard five-day queue instead of the twenty-four-hour one.

A prompt is not a description of the decision logic — it *is* the decision logic, running exactly the way a conditional in source code runs. "Flag as urgent if the damage sounds ongoing and the property sounds occupied" isn't a comment explaining what the system does; it's the actual rule the system is applying, phrased in English instead of code, and every word in it is load-bearing in a way a plain-English sentence normally isn't.

That has two consequences most teams don't act on until something like Aldermere's weekend happens. First, a prompt deserves the discipline a code change gets: a named author, a stated reason for the edit, something resembling review before it goes live — not because prompts are fragile for no reason, but because they're exactly as consequential as the code they're standing in for. Second, and worse: a prompt change almost never fails loudly. The rewritten version still returns a plausible, well-formed answer every time — it doesn't crash, doesn't throw an error, doesn't look different in any dashboard. It just starts deciding differently, for a specific slice of cases, and nothing about the output format changes to tell anyone that happened.

contentSections.scenario:
Three edits are proposed to Aldermere's live triage prompt this week:

(1) A typo fix in an internal instruction line that isn't a category name or an example: "the modle should classify" becomes "the model should classify."

(2) Swapping "homeowner" for "policyholder" throughout the few-shot examples, for tone.

(3) Adding a new required output field, estimatedLossAmount, to the schema the prompt is asked to fill in.
contentSections.question: Which of these need the same review a change to routing code would get, before shipping?

options.label: Only edit 1 — it's the only one touching the instructions directly
Edits 2 and 3 — both can change what the system decides or produces, even though neither touches obviously 'logic-looking' text
None of them — none touch the urgency rule itself, so none are risky

feedback.edit-1-only: Backwards. Edit 1 is the one genuinely safe change here — a typo in an internal instruction line that isn't a category name, an example, or a decision cue doesn't change any output. The two that matter are the ones that look cosmetic and aren't.
feedback.edits-2-3: Right. Edit 2 is exactly the change from the hook — a wording swap in the examples that changes which real claims pattern-match to "urgent," with no visible sign anything changed. Edit 3 changes the output schema the downstream claims system parses, which is a contract change even though it reads as "just adding a field." Both need the same review a code change gets; edit 1 doesn't.
feedback.none: Edit 2 is the exact mechanism that cost Aldermere fourteen unflagged weekend claims — wording in the few-shot examples doubles as the pattern the model matches new claims against, so a tone change is a behavior change. Edit 3 changes what the next system in the pipeline can expect to receive. Neither is safe to ship unreviewed.

contentSections.concept: The prompt is the business logic now. A change to its wording is a change to what gets decided, whether or not the wording looks like a rule — and because a prompt keeps returning a plausible answer regardless, that kind of change fails silently unless it's reviewed before it ships, not after something visibly breaks.

contentSections.title: Reviewing it like the change it is

contentSections.body:
Treating a prompt like a production component doesn't require a heavyweight engineering process. It requires the same minimum a small code change gets anywhere that takes its production system seriously: a named author, one sentence on why the edit is happening, a visible before/after, and a second person looking at that diff before it goes live — not after a client calls about a missed claim.

The reason this matters more for a prompt than for most code is specifically the silent-failure property from the hook. A bad code change usually throws an error, fails a test, or produces an obviously malformed result — something announces itself. A bad prompt change produces another fluent, confident, well-formatted answer, just a differently wrong one. That means the review has to happen on the way in, because there's no reliable signal on the way out that would catch it after.

contentSections.code:
Before: "...if the described damage sounds ongoing and the homeowner mentions being unable to stay in the property, classify as urgent."
After: "...if the described damage sounds ongoing and the policyholder mentions being unable to stay in the property, classify as urgent."

Shipped: edited directly in the shared doc Friday afternoon, no note of why, no one else looked at it before it went live.
contentSections.question: What's the actual flaw in how this change was made — not in the wording itself?

options.label: It shipped without anyone testing what it would change before it went live, and with no record of who changed it or why
"Policyholder" is a worse word choice than "homeowner" for customer-facing tone
The prompt should have been stored as a .txt file instead of in a shared doc

feedback.no-review: Correct. The wording itself isn't the problem — either word could be fine. The problem is that a change capable of shifting urgency classification for a whole category of claims went live with no one checking what it would actually change, no note explaining the intent, and no way to trace who made the edit once the effect showed up two days later.
feedback.worse-tone: Tone preference isn't what caused fourteen claims to sit unflagged over a weekend — the mechanism was pattern-matching against the few-shot examples, not customer-facing politeness. Even a tonally perfect edit made this same way would carry the same risk.
feedback.wrong-format: File format isn't the issue — a shared doc can be reviewed just as rigorously as a text file in version control, and a text file in version control can be edited just as carelessly as a shared doc. What's missing is the review step itself, regardless of where the text lives.

contentSections.flawExplanation: Nothing about swapping one respectful term for another is inherently dangerous. What made it dangerous was shipping it as if it were merely cosmetic: no one asked what the examples' wording was actually doing (anchoring urgency pattern-matching for rental properties), no one compared behavior before and after, and there's no record connecting Monday's backlog to Friday's edit until someone goes looking by hand.

contentSections.body: A prompt edit that changes wording used as a decision cue is a logic change, not a copy edit — it needs the review a code change would get, before it ships, because unlike code it keeps returning a plausible answer even when it's now deciding wrong.

title: Structured output the next step can rely on
description: A prompt that returns a paragraph instead of a schema forces the next step to re-parse prose with a regex — which works until the model phrases the same fact in a new way, and then it fails without anyone noticing.

learningObjectives.text: Identify when free-text output is forcing a downstream system to re-parse prose instead of consume data
Specify a schema with fixed field names and enumerated values that a downstream step can consume without re-parsing

contentSections.title: The paragraph the routing script had to guess at

contentSections.body:
The first version of Aldermere's triage prompt returned a paragraph: "This appears to be an urgent water damage claim requiring immediate attention, given the mention of an active leak and an occupied unit." A small routing script downstream read that paragraph and used a regex looking for phrases like "urgent" or "immediate attention" to decide whether to route the claim to the 24-hour queue.

It worked, for months, on exactly the phrasings the regex had been written against. Then a claim involving a burst pipe in a basement came in, and the model — correctly diagnosing genuine urgency — phrased it differently: "this should be looked at fairly soon given the water is actively spreading." No "urgent." No "immediate attention." The regex found nothing, defaulted to standard priority, and a genuinely urgent claim sat in the five-day queue for four days before a claims adjuster happened to open it early.

The failure wasn't the model's judgment — it correctly recognized the claim as urgent. The failure was asking a downstream system to recover a decision from prose by guessing at phrasing, instead of asking the model to state the decision in a form the next step can consume directly.

The fix is a schema: fixed field names, and for anything the next step branches on, a fixed, enumerated set of allowed values — not free text describing the same idea in whichever words happen to come out. `urgency: "routine" | "priority" | "urgent"` is a value a routing script can switch on directly. "This appears to be an urgent claim requiring immediate attention" is a sentence a routing script has to interpret, and interpretation is exactly where phrasing drift breaks things invisibly. The rule: anything the next step reads to make a decision — a category, a flag, a routing target — gets a named field with a closed set of values. Anything that's genuinely just for a human to read — a one-line rationale, a suggested opening line for the adjuster's reply — can stay as prose, because no downstream code is trying to parse it.

contentSections.problem: Aldermere's claim-triage prompt currently ends with: "Please summarize the claim, note whether it seems urgent, and suggest which category of loss it falls under." Turn this into a specification the downstream claims-intake system can consume without re-parsing prose.

steps.label: Name every field the next step actually branches or stores on
steps.work: The routing script branches on urgency (queue choice) and claimType (which adjuster team). It also stores a human-readable summary for the adjuster to read, but doesn't branch on it.
steps.why: Only fields something downstream reads programmatically need a fixed shape — the human-facing summary doesn't, because nothing is trying to parse it.

steps.label: Give each branching field a closed set of values
steps.work: urgency: one of "routine", "priority", "urgent". claimType: one of "water", "fire", "storm", "theft", "other" — the five categories Aldermere's adjuster teams are actually organized around.
steps.why: A closed set is a value a switch statement can match exactly. An open-ended description ("seems urgent") isn't a value — it's a sentence the routing script would have to interpret, which is where the four-day delay came from.

steps.label: Keep the free-text field, but separate it explicitly
steps.work: summary: a one-to-two sentence plain-language description of the claim, for the adjuster to read — not consumed by any code.
steps.why: This is exactly the kind of field that's fine as prose, because nothing downstream branches on its wording. Mixing it into the same paragraph as the urgency decision was what made the decision hard to extract reliably in the first place.

faded.problem: Aldermere later adds a fourth need: the intake system should flag any claim that mentions a person being hurt, since that routes to a different, regulated process entirely, and it currently has no dedicated field — the model just mentions it in the summary if at all.

blanks.prompt: What kind of field should injuryMentioned be — free text or a closed value — and why?
blanks.why: The routing system needs to branch on this ('does this need the regulated process or not'), which is exactly the case for a fixed value rather than a sentence the routing code would have to search for a mention inside.

blanks.prompt: Where should this field sit relative to the urgency field, given both can independently affect routing?
blanks.answer: As its own separate field, checked independently — not folded into the urgency enum
blanks.why: An injury mention and a high water-damage urgency can both be true of the same claim; collapsing them into one urgency value would force a choice between two facts that need to both be visible to the routing logic.

contentSections.procedure: Before finalizing a prompt's output shape: list what the next step branches on, give each of those a closed set of values, and let only the fields nothing downstream parses stay as free text — checking, as here, whether a new requirement is itself a branching fact that needs its own field, not a mention buried inside another one.

contentSections.title: Enforcing the shape, not just requesting it

contentSections.body:
Asking for a schema in the prompt's instructions is necessary but not sufficient — the model can still occasionally return `"urgency": "quite urgent"` instead of one of the three allowed values, especially under an unusual claim it's less confident about. The next step's contract with the prompt isn't "the model was told to return one of three values"; it's "the intake system validates the returned JSON against the schema before doing anything with it, and rejects or flags anything that doesn't match" — the same way a well-built API validates a request body instead of trusting that callers read the documentation.

That validation step is also where a claim that doesn't cleanly fit any category gets a real, visible outcome — routed to a human with "the model's output didn't validate" as the reason — instead of a routing script quietly doing something undefined with a value it wasn't built to handle.

contentSections.code:
Aldermere's intake system, current version:

result = call_model(claim_text)
urgency = result["urgency"]
queue = URGENT_QUEUE if urgency == "urgent" else STANDARD_QUEUE
route(queue)
contentSections.question: What's missing from this code, given the model is only asked — not guaranteed — to return one of the three defined urgency values?

options.label: Nothing checks that result["urgency"] is actually one of the defined values before using it to route — an unexpected value silently falls into STANDARD_QUEUE
The code should use a slower, more careful model to reduce the chance of an unexpected value
The variable name "urgency" should be renamed to something clearer

feedback.no-validation: Correct. If the model ever returns "quite urgent", "needs review", or anything else outside the three defined values, this code doesn't error — it just isn't equal to "urgent", so it falls through to STANDARD_QUEUE by default, exactly the silent-misroute failure from the hook, just moved one step downstream from the prose-parsing version.
feedback.slower-model: A more careful model reduces how often this happens, but doesn't eliminate it, and the code still has no way to detect it when it does happen. The fix is validating the output, not making the failure rarer while staying equally invisible.
feedback.naming: The variable name isn't the issue — renaming it wouldn't change what happens when the value doesn't match either branch.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A schema in the prompt's instructions is a request, not a guarantee. Without an explicit validation step that checks the returned value is actually one of the defined set — and does something visible when it isn't — an out-of-spec response doesn't fail loudly; it falls through whatever the code's default branch happens to be, which is exactly the kind of quiet misroute a schema was supposed to prevent.

contentSections.body: Anything the next step branches on gets a named field with a closed set of values, validated before it's used — not a sentence the next step has to interpret. Free text is fine for anything a human reads and nothing downstream parses.

title: Examples that pin down the edge cases
description: A few-shot set full of easy, clear-cut claims teaches a model nothing about the genuinely ambiguous ones it will actually see — the examples that matter are the boundary cases pulled from real history, not more of the obvious middle.

learningObjectives.text: Identify which real cases are genuine boundary/edge cases worth pinning down with an example, versus redundant restatements of the easy case
Write a few-shot example that resolves a specific ambiguity the prompt's plain-language instructions leave open

contentSections.title: The claim that was two things at once

contentSections.body:
A storm knocks a tree into the side of a house at one of Aldermere's insured properties. The tree tears a hole in the roof — wind damage — and three days of rain get into the attic through that hole before anyone tarps it — water damage. The claim narrative describes both. Aldermere's triage prompt has a single-select `claimType` field: `"water" | "fire" | "storm" | "theft" | "other"`, and no example in its few-shot set covers a claim that's genuinely two categories at once. The model picks "storm," because the tree is mentioned first — silently routing the claim past the water-damage team's separate check for mold risk and drying timelines, since nothing in the record says water was involved at all.

Separately, a different claim mentions, almost in passing, that a contractor doing emergency board-up work "cut his hand pretty badly" on broken glass. Aldermere's regulatory obligations treat any claim involving a bodily injury as a different track entirely, requiring escalation regardless of property-damage urgency — but nothing in the prompt's instructions or examples ever mentioned injury, so the model treats it as a routine detail in the narrative and classifies the claim on property damage alone.

General instructions describe the common case well and the boundary badly, almost by construction — plain language is good at "usually" and bad at "except when." The fix isn't a longer paragraph of instructions; it's a few-shot example placed at exactly the boundary that's ambiguous, showing the model what to do with the specific case the instructions alone don't resolve.

That means the examples worth adding aren't drawn from Aldermere's easiest, most common claims — a straightforward burst pipe with no complications teaches the model almost nothing it doesn't already handle correctly. The examples worth adding are pulled from the real, specific cases where the current prompt got it wrong or where a human reviewer had to think about it: the multi-peril claim, the injury mentioned in passing, the claim where "urgent" is genuinely a judgment call. Each one earns its place by resolving an ambiguity the instructions leave open — not by restating the easy case in different words.

contentSections.scenario: Aldermere's few-shot set currently has eleven examples. Reviewing them against the module's principle — each example should resolve a specific ambiguity, not restate the easy case — here's what's actually in the set.
contentSections.question: Select every example that's earning its place — genuinely resolving an ambiguity the plain-language instructions don't cover on their own.

items.label: A claim describing both wind damage from a fallen tree and water intrusion through the resulting hole, labeled claimType: ["storm", "water"], showing the field can hold more than one value
A claim mentioning a contractor's hand injury during emergency repairs, labeled injuryMentioned: true and routed to the regulated track regardless of the property-damage urgency
A textbook burst-pipe claim with no complications, clearly urgent, clearly claimType: "water" — the fourth example in the set showing essentially this same pattern

A claim where the homeowner describes 'some water stains' with no mention of an active leak or occupancy status, labeled urgency: "priority" rather than "urgent", with a note on what tipped the judgment call
A claim example chosen specifically because the homeowner wrote an unusually clear, well-organized narrative
A second straightforward fire-damage claim added because the first fire example 'felt a little short'

explanation.multi-peril: Applicable. This is exactly the ambiguity the instructions don't resolve on their own — whether the field can hold two true values at once — and the tree-and-rain claim from the hook shows precisely why leaving it unresolved routes claims wrong.
explanation.injury-mention: Applicable. Nothing in the plain-language instructions told the model that an injury mentioned in passing, unrelated to the claim's main property-damage narrative, still triggers a mandatory different track. This example is the only place that rule actually gets pinned down.
explanation.clear-burst-pipe: Not applicable, and it's the fourth example doing the same job as the first three. A clean, unambiguous case the model already classifies correctly teaches nothing new — the set already had three of these before this one was added.
explanation.ambiguous-urgent: Applicable. "Some water stains" with no stated active leak or occupancy is a genuine judgment call between priority and urgent, and showing which way it resolves, with the reasoning, is exactly the kind of boundary the plain instructions leave open.
explanation.well-written-narrative: Not applicable. How clearly the homeowner happened to write isn't a source of ambiguity in classification — it doesn't teach the model anything about a decision it was getting wrong.
explanation.another-fire-clear: Not applicable, and "felt a little short" is a tell — an example added to round out a category rather than to resolve a specific case the model handled badly is padding, even when the underlying claim is real.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six examples earn their place because each resolves a specific ambiguity the plain-language instructions leave open: a multi-label case, an out-of-band regulatory trigger, and a genuine judgment call on the boundary between two urgency levels. The other three are redundant restatements of a case the model already handles — writing quality, category padding, or a fourth version of the easy case add length to the prompt without adding anything the model didn't already know.

contentSections.title: Finding the next example worth writing

contentSections.body:
The source for new examples isn't imagination — it's the record of what the current prompt actually got wrong. Every time a human reviewer overrides the model's classification, or a claim comes back for a second look, that's a candidate boundary case: what did the model do, what should it have done, and what about the instructions failed to say why. A running log of these — even an informal one — turns "add more examples" from a guess into a targeted fix aimed at the model's actual failure pattern, the same discipline the next lesson's test set formalizes.

There's a real cost to over-adding, too: every example in the prompt costs tokens and, past a certain density, can start crowding out the plain-language instructions' influence in favor of pattern-matching too literally to the examples given. The discipline cuts both ways — add an example because it resolves a real, recurring ambiguity; don't add one because the set feels thin.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in the order that turns a real classification miss into a useful few-shot example, rather than a guess at what might help.
steps: Notice a claim where a human reviewer overrode the model's classification
Identify exactly which ambiguity in the instructions let the model get it wrong
Check whether an existing example already covers this ambiguity, or if it's genuinely new
Write the new example using the real claim's specifics, labeled with the reviewer's correct classification
Re-run the prompt against the existing test set to confirm the new example didn't change other classifications
contentSections.explanation: Noticing the override comes first because that's the actual signal — not a hunch about what might be ambiguous. Naming the specific ambiguity (not just "the model got this wrong") is what turns the miss into something an example can fix; without it, the new example risks teaching the wrong lesson. Checking for an existing near-duplicate prevents the padding problem from the evidence-stack. Using the real claim's specifics, not a cleaned-up hypothetical, is what makes the example representative of what the model will actually see. The final step is the one skipped under time pressure, and it's the whole subject of this module's last lesson — a new example can fix one case while quietly breaking another.

contentSections.body: Few-shot examples earn their place by resolving a specific ambiguity the plain-language instructions leave open — pulled from real cases the current prompt actually got wrong, not invented, and not more restatements of the case it already handles.

title: Versioning prompts and knowing which one ran
description: A regulator asking which criteria classified a specific claim six months ago is asking a question that only has an answer if every decision the prompt made was logged against the exact prompt version that made it.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why a decision made by a prompt needs its prompt version logged alongside it, not just the output
Design a version-and-decision log that lets a specific past classification be reconstructed and defended

contentSections.body:
Six months after Aldermere's triage prompt went live, a state insurance regulator conducting a routine audit asks a specific question: for claim #48213, filed in March and classified "routine" at the time, what exactly were the criteria that produced that classification? It's a fair question — a claimant is disputing the five-day wait, and the regulator wants to see the reasoning was consistent with Aldermere's stated triage policy.

Nobody can answer it. The prompt has been edited four times since March, directly in the same shared doc, each time overwriting the previous version with no saved history. The current prompt's wording is different enough that running claim #48213's text through it today produces a different classification than what actually shipped in March — but there's no way to know if that's because the claim was genuinely borderline or because the prompt itself changed. Aldermere can't reconstruct what ran, so it can't defend what happened.

Every AI-made decision that might ever need to be explained — to a regulator, a client, or an internal reviewer — needs two things logged alongside it, not one: the output, and *exactly which version of the prompt produced it*. Logging only the output answers "what did the system decide"; it can't answer "was that decision consistent with policy," because there's no fixed reference point to check the decision against.

The practice is straightforward and doesn't require heavy tooling: give every shipped prompt a version identifier (a simple sequential tag is enough — v1, v2, v3), store the full text of each version somewhere it can't be silently overwritten, and log the version identifier alongside every decision it makes, together with the model name and the input that was actually sent. Treat a prompt exactly the way a codebase treats a release: each version is a fixed, retrievable artifact, and "which version ran on this date" is always a knowable, answerable question — not a reconstruction project six months later.

contentSections.intro: Specify what Aldermere's decision log needs to record for every triage classification, so a claim like #48213 can be fully reconstructed later. Four fields.

fields.prompt: What identifies exactly which prompt text produced this decision?

options.label: a version tag (e.g. "v3") pointing to a stored, immutable copy of that exact prompt text
the date the decision was made

feedback.version-tag: Right — a date alone doesn't tell you which prompt was live on that date if the prompt changed more than once that week, and it gives nothing to compare against if the prompt was edited and reverted.
feedback.just-date: This is the trap Aldermere fell into. A date only helps if there's a record of exactly which prompt version was live at that moment — without a stored, versioned copy to point to, the date alone reconstructs nothing.

fields.prompt: Where does the actual text of each prompt version live?

options.label: a store where a shipped version, once tagged, can never be silently overwritten by the next edit
the same shared doc, since anyone can always scroll back through edit history informally

feedback.immutable-store: Right — this is exactly what Aldermere's shared doc didn't have. Each version needs to be a fixed, retrievable artifact once it ships, not a snapshot that depends on nobody having edited over it since.
feedback.shared-doc: This is what actually happened at Aldermere, four times over, with no saved history — by the time the regulator asked, the March version simply didn't exist anywhere to be checked.

fields.prompt: Besides the prompt version, what else has to be logged to fully reconstruct a decision?

options.label: the exact model name/version used, and the exact input text the prompt was run on
just the final output — the prompt version is enough on its own

feedback.model-and-input: Right — the same prompt run on a different model, or the same prompt run on a slightly different extraction of the claim text, can produce a different result. Full reconstruction needs all three: prompt version, model version, and the actual input.
feedback.output-only: The prompt version alone tells you what rules were supposed to apply, not what was actually fed into them or which model executed them — both of which can change the outcome independent of the prompt text itself.

fields.prompt: What does "can be fully reconstructed later" actually require of this log?

options.label: any single claim's decision, plus its exact prompt version, model, and input, can be pulled up and re-examined months later without depending on anyone's memory
a general sense that the system was working correctly around that time

feedback.retrievable: Right — this is the actual bar the regulator's question set. "We believe it was working correctly" isn't a defense; being able to pull up claim #48213 specifically and show exactly what ran is.
feedback.general-sense: This is roughly where Aldermere ended up — confident the system was generally reasonable, with no way to answer the specific question actually asked about one specific claim.

contentSections.synthesis: Together these four decisions describe a log where any single past decision — not just the system in general — can be pulled up and defended on its own terms: which exact prompt ran, stored somewhere it couldn't be silently overwritten, on which model, against which input. That's the difference between "we're confident it was fine" and "here is exactly what happened, and why."

contentSections.body:
Versioning solves the audit-trail problem; it doesn't solve the review problem from the module's first lesson, and it's worth being clear about the difference. Giving every edit a version number means "which prompt ran on March 14th" always has an answer — it does not by itself mean every edit was reviewed before it shipped. A team can version-tag a careless, unreviewed change just as easily as a careful one; the tag records what happened, it doesn't gate what's allowed to happen.

The two practices work together: review (the first lesson) is the gate before a version ships; the version log (this lesson) is the record after it has. A prompt-as-production-component discipline needs both — skipping review because "it's versioned, so we can always check what happened" answers the regulator's question after the fact while doing nothing to prevent the fourteen unflagged claims in the first place.

Log the prompt version, model, and exact input alongside every decision, with each shipped version stored somewhere it can't be silently overwritten — versioning answers "what ran and why" months later, but it's a record after the fact, not a substitute for reviewing a change before it ships.

title: Changing a prompt without breaking what worked
description: Fixing the one edge case a prompt gets wrong, without checking what the fix does to every case it already got right, is how a targeted improvement quietly becomes a regression nobody notices until a client complains.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why testing a prompt revision only against the case it was meant to fix is insufficient
Design a before/after regression comparison against a full gold set before shipping a prompt revision

contentSections.title: The fix that broke something else

contentSections.body:
Aldermere's storm-claim classifications have been slightly off — the model keeps under-labeling multi-peril storm claims (wind and water together) as just "storm," missing the water-team's mold-risk check, roughly the pattern from the earlier lesson. The consultant rewrites the instruction around multi-peril claims to be more explicit: "if the narrative describes damage from more than one cause, list every applicable claimType." She tests it against the three multi-peril claims she has on hand, gets the right answer on all three, and ships it the same afternoon.

Two weeks later, a claims manager flags a different problem: water-damage claims that mention "the pipes" for any reason at all — including several routine claims where the narrative just mentions checking the pipes as part of describing the plumbing layout — are now getting labeled `["water", "storm"]` even when there's no storm involved anywhere in the claim. The more explicit multi-peril instruction, tuned to catch the case it was meant to fix, made the model over-eager to apply multiple labels generally, and nobody caught it because the only thing tested was the case the change targeted.

A revision that's tested only against the case that motivated it answers one question — "did this fix what I was trying to fix" — and leaves a much more important one unasked: "did this change anything else." A prompt is one connected set of instructions and examples; a wording change made for one purpose can shift the model's behavior on cases that had nothing to do with the original problem, the same way Aldermere's "friendlier tone" edit shifted urgency classification through a completely different mechanism than the one it was made for.

The fix is a gold set: a standing collection of real, already-classified past cases — spanning the easy cases, the resolved edge cases from earlier examples, and anything a human has previously had to correct — that every candidate revision gets run against in full, before shipping, regardless of how narrow the intended fix was. The comparison that matters isn't "does the new version get the target case right" — it's "where do the old and new versions disagree across the whole set, and is every disagreement an improvement."

contentSections.scenario: Aldermere's gold set has 40 past claims with known-correct classifications. The consultant runs both the old and new multi-peril prompt against all 40. 38 classifications are identical between versions. Two differ: one is the multi-peril storm claim the fix was meant to catch (now correct, previously wrong) — an improvement. The other is a routine plumbing-inspection claim with no storm or water damage, now labeled ["water", "storm"] where the old version correctly labeled it ["other"] — a new error the fix introduced.
contentSections.question: What does this comparison reveal that testing only against the three multi-peril claims wouldn't have?

options.label: That the fix genuinely improved one case while introducing a new, different error in an unrelated case — a trade worth seeing and deciding on explicitly before shipping
That the new prompt is strictly worse and should be discarded entirely
Nothing new — three targeted tests and forty gold-set tests would show the same result

feedback.regression-visible: Correct. Running the full gold set surfaces exactly the trade the narrow test missed: a real fix to the intended case, alongside a new, unrelated error the narrow test had no way to catch since it only had multi-peril claims in it. That's a decision the consultant can now make deliberately — tighten the new instruction further, or ship it and separately fix the plumbing-mention over-eagerness — instead of shipping blind.
feedback.discard: One new error against one genuine fix isn't automatically a worse trade — it depends on how common each case actually is in Aldermere's real claim volume.
