The point of the full comparison isn't to force a discard; it's to make the trade-off visible so it can be weighed, rather than shipping without knowing it exists at all.
feedback.nothing-new: The three-claim test, by construction, only contained multi-peril cases — it had no routine plumbing-mention claim in it to reveal the new error on. A test set that can only contain the target case can only ever confirm the target case improved; it structurally cannot catch a regression outside its own scope.

contentSections.mechanism: The multi-peril instruction was tuned on multi-peril examples, so it improved exactly the pattern it was shown — and the more explicit language about "more than one cause" made the model more willing to attach a second label generally, including to claims that merely mention a second topic (pipes) without describing damage from it. A test set narrow enough to only contain the target case cannot, by definition, detect a side effect that falls outside it.

contentSections.title: Deciding what to do with a real trade-off

contentSections.body:
Finding a regression before shipping isn't the end of the process — it's the point where a real decision gets made instead of an accidental one. Three honest paths exist once a full gold-set run shows a trade-off: tighten the revision further and re-run the full comparison again (the routine path — most first-draft fixes are slightly too broad); ship anyway if the fixed case is common and costly and the new error is rare and low-stakes, with the new error logged as a known, accepted gap rather than a surprise; or don't ship, if the new error is worse than the problem being solved.

What makes any of these defensible is that the trade-off was seen and chosen, against the full set, before the change went live — not discovered by a claims manager two weeks later. The discipline costs one extra step (running the full set instead of just the target case); the alternative costs a live regression running silently until someone notices.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in order for shipping a prompt revision without repeating Aldermere's plumbing-claim regression.
steps: Identify the specific case the revision is meant to fix
Write and test the revision against that specific case until it's correct
Run the full gold set — not just the target case — against both the old and new prompt versions
Review every case where the two versions disagree, not just the ones that improved
Decide explicitly: tighten further, ship with a logged known gap, or don't ship
Version and log the shipped revision per the previous lesson's practice
contentSections.explanation: The target case comes first because that's the actual motivation for the change, and there's no point running a full comparison against a revision that doesn't even fix what it was meant to. The full gold-set run is the step Aldermere's consultant skipped, and it's what turns an invisible side effect into a visible one. Reviewing every disagreement — not filtering to the improvements — is what surfaces the plumbing-claim regression rather than declaring victory after seeing the multi-peril fix land. The explicit decision step is what makes shipping a choice instead of an accident. Versioning last connects this lesson back to the previous one: a shipped revision, even a deliberately imperfect one, still needs to be a retrievable, logged artifact.

contentSections.body: Test a prompt revision against the full gold set, not just the case that motivated it — a fix tuned to one problem can quietly shift behavior on cases that had nothing to do with it, and the only way to see that before a client does is to look at everything the old and new versions disagree on.

title: Practice — Convert Seven Ad-Hoc Prompts into Specified Components
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given an ad-hoc prompt or a shipping decision about one, apply this module's review, schema, examples, versioning and regression-testing distinctions.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's structured-output and edge-case-example distinctions to new prompts
Decide whether a prompt change is safe to ship as described, using this module's review and regression criteria

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Build and Version a Production Prompt with a Test Set
description: Specify a prompt for a real or realistic classification/extraction task, build a gold test set including deliberate edge cases, log a baseline run, make one deliberate revision, and compare before and after against the full set.

learningObjectives.text: Specify a prompt with structured, validated output and edge-case examples for a real task
Build and run a gold test set, then regression-test one deliberate revision against it before treating it as shippable

contentSections.body: Every discipline in this module got real the moment it was tested against actual cases instead of a clean demo. That's the lab: pick one classification or extraction task — from your own work, a client's, or a plausible one you can specify concretely — and take it through the full cycle: a schema, edge-case examples, a version-tagged baseline, and one deliberate revision tested against the whole set before it ships.

contentSections.title: Your versioned production prompt
contentSections.brief: Pick one specific classification or extraction task where a prompt's output needs to be consumed reliably by something downstream — a system, a spreadsheet, a human following a fixed process. You're going to specify its output schema, write a first version with edge-case examples, log a baseline run against a real test set, then make one deliberate revision and prove, with evidence, what it changed and didn't.
contentSections.deliverable: A versioned prompt (v1 and v2), its test set including deliberate edge cases, a baseline run log, and a before/after comparison of the revision against the full test set with the trade-off decision stated explicitly.

stages.title: Specify the task and its output schema
stages.instructions: Name the task concretely — not 'classify tickets' but the actual categories, the actual downstream consumer, and what it does with each field. For every field the downstream consumer branches on, define a closed set of allowed values; for anything purely human-facing, leave it as free text and say so explicitly.
stages.checkpoint: You have a schema with every branching field enumerated, and a one-line note on why each free-text field is safe to leave open.

stages.title: Write prompt v1 and assemble a test set with real edge cases
stages.instructions: Write the prompt's instructions and 3-5 few-shot examples. Assemble 10-15 test cases, including at least three deliberately ambiguous or boundary cases (the kind this module's lessons were built around) — not just clean, easy examples. Label each with the classification you believe is correct and why.
stages.checkpoint: You have a labeled test set where at least three cases are genuinely ambiguous, not obviously easy.

stages.title: Run and log the v1 baseline
stages.instructions: Run v1 against every test case. Log the result for each one, including the misses — don't discard or explain away a wrong classification before it's logged. Tag this as v1 and record it somewhere it won't be silently overwritten.
stages.checkpoint: You have a logged result for every test case, with every miss visible, tagged to prompt version v1.

stages.title: Make one deliberate revision and regression-test it
stages.instructions: Pick one real miss from the baseline and revise the prompt to fix it — instructions, an added example, or both. Run the full test set again against v2, not just the case you targeted. Compare every case where v1 and v2 disagree, and write an explicit decision: ship, tighten further, or don't ship.
stages.checkpoint: You have a full before/after comparison across the whole test set, with every disagreement reviewed and a stated shipping decision.

rubric.criterion: The task and consumer are stated concretely
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the task could name exactly what's being classified, who or what consumes the output, and what each field is used for.

rubric.criterion: Every branching field has a closed set of values; free-text fields are justified
rubric.meets: The schema names which fields are enumerated and which are free text, with a stated reason for each free-text field.

rubric.criterion: The test set includes genuine edge cases, not only easy ones
rubric.meets: At least three test cases are ambiguous enough that a careful human might disagree on the label, and the reasoning for the chosen label is written down.

rubric.criterion: The v1 baseline is logged completely, including misses
rubric.meets: Every test case has a recorded v1 result, with wrong classifications visible rather than omitted.

rubric.criterion: The revision is regression-tested against the full set, not just its target case
rubric.meets: The comparison covers every test case, not only the one the revision was meant to fix, and every disagreement between v1 and v2 is listed.

rubric.criterion: The shipping decision is explicit and reasoned
rubric.meets: The write-up states ship, tighten, or don't-ship, with the trade-off (if any) named rather than implied.

contentSections.body: A prompt tested against its own gold set, before and after a real revision, is the only version of "it works" you're entitled to put a version number on.

title: Checkpoint — Prompts as Production Components
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from three modules back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's prompt-as-production distinctions, and earlier modules' pipeline-design and risk-framing distinctions, without looking them up

questions.from: This module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: A teammate rewords Aldermere's triage prompt for tone, swapping "homeowner" for "policyholder" throughout the examples, and ships it without review because it "didn't touch the actual instructions." What did this change actually do?

options.label: Nothing meaningful — tone wording doesn't affect classification
It shifted which claims pattern-matched to the urgent examples, quietly under-flagging rental-property claims over a weekend
It made the prompt run slower

questions.explanation: The word "homeowner" was functioning as an incidental urgency signal in the few-shot examples — removing it from claims naming a tenant made those claims pattern-match less strongly to "urgent," leaving fourteen real claims unflagged with no visible error anywhere.

questions.from: This module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: Aldermere's routing script used to search a paragraph of prose for words like "urgent" to decide which queue a claim went to. What replaced that approach, and why?

options.label: A longer paragraph with more urgency-related keywords included
A named field with a closed set of values (like urgency: "urgent") that the routing script reads directly instead of guessing at from phrasing
A human reading every claim before routing it

questions.explanation: The regex-based approach broke the moment the model phrased urgency in new words it hadn't been tested against. A closed enumerated field removes the guessing entirely — the routing script reads a defined value instead of interpreting prose.

questions.from: This module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: Why did adding examples of Aldermere's clean, unambiguous burst-pipe claim — a fourth time — not improve the prompt?

options.label: Because the model already classified that case correctly, so the example taught it nothing new, while adding length that diluted the examples that did resolve real ambiguity
Because burst-pipe claims should never be used as examples
Because four examples is always too many for one prompt

questions.explanation: A useful example resolves a genuine ambiguity the instructions leave open. A case the model already handles correctly, repeated, is padding — it costs length without teaching anything, which is exactly why the multi-peril and injury-mention examples (which did resolve real ambiguity) mattered more.

questions.from: This module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: A regulator asks what criteria classified a specific claim from six months ago, and Aldermere can't answer, because the prompt had been edited four times since with no saved history. What would have made this answerable?

options.label: A version tag and immutably stored copy of every shipped prompt, logged alongside the model and exact input for every decision it made
A stricter word limit on how long the prompt could be
Editing the prompt less frequently

questions.explanation: The problem wasn't edit frequency — it was that no past version was preserved and no decision was logged against a specific version. A version-tagged, immutably stored prompt, referenced in every decision log, makes "what ran on this date" always answerable regardless of how often the prompt changes.

questions.from: Previous module — Designing the Pipeline
questions.prompt: Per the previous module, what actually went wrong when Fennimore's extraction step wrote straight into the dispatch system tagged "needs review," with review happening afterward?

options.label: The tender became real and bookable before anyone reviewed it — the review happened after the consequential step, not before it
Extraction was too slow
Dispatchers shouldn't have been reviewing tenders at all

questions.explanation: This was a sequencing flaw in the pipeline design, not an accuracy problem — the write step with real consequences ran before the gate meant to catch a wrong extraction.

questions.from: Previous module — Designing the Pipeline
questions.prompt: What did the previous module say a step contract needs to make explicit, per the mismatch between one engineer's "rate" field and another's expected "totalRate" field?

options.label: Exactly what one step guarantees to produce and what the next step requires to receive, in writing, not assumed
Which engineer is responsible for the whole pipeline
A shared programming language for every step

questions.explanation: Both steps worked correctly in isolation — the actual gap was an unwritten handoff contract, the same category of problem this module's structured-output lesson addresses one level down, inside a single step's own output.

questions.from: Previous module — Designing the Pipeline
questions.prompt: Why did Fennimore's overnight batch job produce 40 duplicate bookings after crashing and automatically restarting at item 40 of 70?

options.label: It lacked idempotency — nothing made re-running the same batch safe, so the restart redid work it had already completed
The network connection was too slow
The batch size was too large

questions.explanation: A crash-and-restart is expected for an unattended overnight job; the real gap was that re-running wasn't safe, because the job had no way to recognize which items it had already processed.

questions.from: Previous module — Designing the Pipeline
questions.prompt: During a short model-provider outage with a nine-hour runway before the next batch ran, what was the right response, per the previous module?

options.label: Let the affected items wait in the queue with retry-and-backoff, since the fallback should match the actual urgency and runway, not trigger automatically
Immediately route everything to manual entry regardless of urgency
Do nothing and assume the pipeline handles it without a deliberately built behavior

questions.explanation: Matching the fallback to actual urgency meant the short outage didn't need an expensive manual fallback — but only because retry-and-queue was a deliberately designed behavior, not an assumption.

questions.from: Three modules back — Naming the Risk Before You Commit
questions.prompt: Per the risk-framing module, why does a proposal's risk section listing only generic categories ("model accuracy may vary," "data privacy must be maintained") fail to do its job?

options.label: Because it doesn't name plausible, specific failure modes for this particular process and client — Anchorline's actual exclusion, buried in a document the model never saw, wasn't covered by either generic line
Because risk sections should never be included in proposals at all
Because it was too short to be taken seriously

questions.explanation: Generic risk categories are true of almost any AI project and specific to none of them — they wouldn't have prompted anyone to check whether the model had actually been shown every policy exclusion, which is what let Anchorline's loan-modification tool wrongly approve an excluded loan type.

questions.from: Three modules back — Naming the Risk Before You Commit
questions.prompt: Two designs for Anchorline's triage tool reach the same 3% measured error rate. Per that module, why aren't they equally risky?

options.label: One fails loudly (a visible flag routes low-confidence cases to a monitored queue) and one fails silently (a wrong decision looks identical to a right one) — the silent design leaves errors uncaught for far longer
They are equally risky, since the error rate is what determines risk
The louder design is riskier because it creates more visible complaints

questions.explanation: Equal error rates can carry very different risk depending on whether a wrong decision announces itself — a distinction that also underlies this module's insistence on validating structured output rather than trusting it silently, so a bad value doesn't fall through to a default branch unnoticed.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The existing systems are the constraint, not the background
description: A pipeline design sketched before anyone checks what the client's existing system actually allows is a design for a system that doesn't exist — the real one has to be discovered first, and it sets the boundary everything else fits inside.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an automation's existing target systems are a primary design constraint rather than context to work around later
Distinguish a discovery finding that genuinely constrains the design from one that doesn't

contentSections.title: The architecture that assumed an API

contentSections.body:
Corrigan & Vale Pharmacy Group wants patient refill requests — arriving by fax, an online portal, and a pharmacy app — triaged and queued for pharmacist review automatically instead of retyped by hand at each of its seven locations. Before the first working session, the consultant sketches a clean architecture: intake tool extracts the request, calls the dispensing system's API to check for drug interactions and insurance status, then writes a pending order directly into the queue.

In the first working session, Corrigan & Vale's IT contractor explains what ScriptLedger — the dispensing system every location has run for over twenty years — actually is: no API of any kind. The only programmatic access is a nightly batch export of yesterday's filled prescriptions. It runs on a single on-premises Windows server per location that the contractor is visibly nervous about touching, because a different vendor's "lightweight" monitoring agent, installed two years ago, crashed the server for six hours during a Tuesday afternoon dispensing rush. The clean architecture assumed a system that doesn't exist.

The design sketched before discovery wasn't wrong because the consultant was careless — it was wrong because it was built on an assumption instead of a fact, and that's the actual failure mode this lesson is about. An automation doesn't get to specify what the existing systems provide; it has to work inside what they actually provide, discovered first, before a pipeline gets drawn or a tool gets chosen.

That makes "what does the existing system actually allow" the first real question of any integration engagement, not a detail confirmed once the design is mostly done. ScriptLedger's missing API, its one nightly export, and its fragile server aren't obstacles to route around after the fact — they're the boundary the whole design has to fit inside, the same way this track's earlier module on data readiness treated what data genuinely exists, in what shape, as the boundary an automation has to respect rather than wish past.

contentSections.scenario: More discovery findings surface in the same session: (1) ScriptLedger has no API. (2) The server is a single on-premises machine per location, not a shared cloud instance. (3) The pharmacy's front-desk staff currently wear blue polo shirts as a dress code. (4) A previous vendor's monitoring agent crashed the server for six hours.
contentSections.question: Which of these findings actually constrain the integration design, versus being true but irrelevant to it?

options.label: All four equally — every fact learned in discovery should shape the design
Findings 1, 2 and 4 — the missing API, the single fragile per-location server, and the prior crash all bound what's safe or possible to build; the dress code doesn't
Only finding 1 — the missing API is the only fact that matters

feedback.all-four: Discovery surfaces plenty of true facts that don't bound the design — the dress code has no bearing on how software talks to ScriptLedger. Treating every fact as equally load-bearing makes it harder to see which ones actually matter.
feedback.one-two-four: Right. The missing API sets what kind of access is even possible. The single per-location server (not a shared, resilient cloud instance) sets how cautious any new software running near it needs to be. The prior crash is direct evidence of that server's fragility under load — it's not just a hypothetical risk, it already happened. The dress code is true and irrelevant.
feedback.one-only: The missing API matters, but it's not the whole picture — a fragile single server with a documented history of being crashed by new software is just as real a constraint on what's safe to deploy, even for an integration that doesn't touch the API question at all.

contentSections.concept: The existing systems are the constraint, not the background — but that means specifically the facts that bound what's possible or safe, discovered before the design is drawn, not every fact discovery happens to turn up.

contentSections.title: Designing after discovery, not before it

contentSections.body:
Getting the order right matters as much as getting the content right. A pipeline sketch, a tool shortlist, or a written proposal produced before this kind of discovery session isn't a draft to refine — it's a guess about a system nobody has actually looked at yet, and every hour spent detailing it is an hour spent on a plan that a twenty-minute conversation with IT can invalidate.

The discipline this lesson asks for is small and concrete: before drawing anything, name what the target system actually offers for reading data, writing data, and running new software near it, confirmed by someone who administers it — not assumed from how a comparable modern system usually works. ScriptLedger not having an API isn't unusual for a twenty-year-old pharmacy dispensing system; assuming otherwise is the mistake, not the system's age.

contentSections.code:
Proposal excerpt, written before the discovery session:

"The intake tool will call ScriptLedger's API to verify insurance status in real time before queuing each refill request, ensuring pharmacists always see current coverage information."
contentSections.question: What's the flaw in this proposal line, independent of whether real-time insurance verification is a good idea?

options.label: It commits to a specific integration mechanism (a real-time API call) that was never confirmed to exist on the target system
Real-time insurance verification is never a useful feature to build
The sentence is too long for a proposal

feedback.unconfirmed-api: Correct. This line describes a capability ScriptLedger doesn't have — there's no API to call in real time. Writing it into a proposal before confirming it with whoever administers the system means promising something the target system can't deliver, discovered only once the client is already relying on the proposal.
feedback.feature-bad: The feature itself might be exactly what Corrigan & Vale needs — the flaw isn't the goal, it's building a specific mechanism into a commitment before checking whether that mechanism is available on the actual system.
feedback.too-long: Sentence length isn't the issue here — a much shorter sentence promising the same unavailable capability would carry the identical problem.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A proposal line describing a specific technical mechanism — "the API," "real time" — is a factual claim about what the target system supports, not aspirational language. Writing it before discovery confirms the mechanism exists is the same mistake as the architecture sketch from the hook: designing for the system that would make the engagement easiest, rather than the one that's actually there.

contentSections.body: What the existing systems actually allow — confirmed by whoever administers them, not assumed — is the boundary the whole design fits inside, discovered before anything gets drawn, priced, or promised.

title: APIs, exports, and the system with neither
description: ScriptLedger offers no API, a nightly export that's always a day stale, and a manually-triggered PDF dump of today's queue — three genuinely different integration tiers, and the right one depends on how much delay the task can actually tolerate, not on which is technically most impressive.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish real API, scheduled export/batch, and no-programmatic-access as integration tiers with different latency and reliability properties
Match an integration tier to a task's actual tolerance for data staleness

contentSections.body:
Cataloging ScriptLedger's real access surface, location by location: no API, full stop. A nightly batch export — a CSV of yesterday's filled prescriptions, generated automatically at 2 a.m., always describing data that's already at least a day old by the time anyone reads it. And a "print pending orders" feature: a staff member can manually trigger a PDF dump of whatever's currently in today's queue, with no schedule, no notification, and no guarantee anyone remembers to run it.

None of these three lets the intake tool see a live, current view of today's queue on demand. The nightly export is a day behind by design. The PDF dump is current but only exists at the moment someone happens to trigger it, and nothing tells the automation when that happens. Whatever gets built has to be designed around one of these three, not around a live connection that doesn't exist.

Three integration tiers show up on almost every engagement, and they're genuinely different, not just different implementations of the same idea. A **real API** is live and structured — read and often write access on demand, the ideal case, and rare on systems this age. A **scheduled export or batch file** is structured but always stale by however long the schedule's interval is — perfectly fine for anything that can tolerate that delay, actively wrong for anything that can't. **Nothing at all** means either RPA driving the system's own screen the way a person would — genuinely useful where nothing else exists, and fragile in the specific way this track covered earlier: it breaks the moment the screen layout changes — or accepting that a human has to bridge the gap manually for that specific step.

The decision isn't "which tier sounds most sophisticated" — a batch export isn't a downgrade from an API, it's the correct match for a task that genuinely doesn't need up-to-the-minute data. The question that actually decides it: how much delay can this specific task tolerate before the delay itself becomes the problem? A nightly report of yesterday's completed dispenses tolerates the export tier fine. A pharmacist needing to know, right now, whether a refill request has already been filled today does not.

contentSections.scenario:
Corrigan & Vale has four separate needs for the new intake tool. The consultant is deciding which integration tier fits each.

(A) A weekly report to the pharmacy owner summarizing total refills processed per location.
(B) Checking, at the moment a refill request comes in, whether that same prescription was already filled today by walk-in, to avoid double-dispensing.
(C) Letting a pharmacist glance at a dashboard showing roughly how the day's queue is trending.
(D) Confirming, before queuing a request, that the prescription hasn't expired according to yesterday's most recent fill record.
contentSections.question: Select every need where the nightly batch export is actually a defensible fit, not a compromise being made because nothing better exists.

items.label: (A) The weekly owner report — built entirely from a week of nightly exports, with no need for anything more current
(B) The same-day double-dispense check — a day-old export can't show whether the prescription was filled earlier today
(C) The rough daily-trend dashboard — "roughly how the day is trending" doesn't require current-to-the-minute figures
(D) The expiry check against yesterday's most recent fill record — expiry status changes slowly, so a one-day-old record is accurate for this purpose almost all the time

explanation.weekly-report: Applicable. A weekly report has no requirement for current-day data at all — seven nightly exports assembled after the fact is not a compromise, it's a complete match for what the report needs.
explanation.double-dispense-check: Not applicable, and this is the dangerous one. The nightly export can't see anything filled today — using it here means the check would systematically miss same-day double-dispenses, the exact case it exists to catch. This need requires the PDF-dump tier at minimum, ideally a same-day check some other way.
explanation.dashboard-trending: Applicable. "Roughly trending" is explicitly tolerant of staleness — a dashboard built on yesterday's completed volume, refreshed nightly, is an honest fit for a rough-trend view, not a corner cut.
explanation.expiry-check: Applicable, with a caveat worth stating out loud in the design: expiry dates don't change hour to hour, so a fill record that's up to a day old is accurate for this specific check the overwhelming majority of the time. It's a defensible fit precisely because the task's tolerance for staleness happens to match the export's actual staleness.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the four needs are genuine fits for the nightly export, and one — same-day double-dispense checking — structurally cannot be served by a source that's always at least a day behind. The distinction isn't about which need is more important; it's about which needs can tolerate a day of staleness and which can't, and matching the tier to that answer rather than defaulting to whatever access already exists.

contentSections.body:
The same-day double-dispense check from the evidence-stack has no good source in ScriptLedger's existing access — not the nightly export (too stale) and not really the ad-hoc PDF dump either, since nothing tells the automation when a fresh one has been triggered or ensures one exists for the moment a refill request arrives. This is the case where "nothing at all" is the honest answer, and the choice becomes RPA versus a human step, not which existing export to lean on harder.

RPA — driving ScriptLedger's own screen the way a pharmacy technician would, to query today's fill status directly — is a real option here, and it's the case this track's earlier tool-selection work described it for: a system with no API that genuinely needs a same-day answer. It's also fragile in exactly the way already established — it breaks the moment ScriptLedger's screen layout changes, which for a twenty-year-old system on an aging Windows server is a real, recurring maintenance cost, not a hypothetical one. The alternative — a technician manually checking before confirming a refill — is slower but doesn't break silently. Which one is right depends on the volume of refills this check actually needs to run against and how much a technician's time is worth relative to the maintenance cost of a screen-driving bot; there's no default answer that's automatically correct.

Real API, scheduled export, and no access at all are genuinely different tiers, not a ladder to climb — match the tier to how much delay the specific task can tolerate, and when nothing fits, choose deliberately between RPA's fragility and a human step's slowness rather than defaulting to whichever access already happens to exist.

title: Identity, access and whose account it runs as
description: Running an automation under a shared login with a pharmacist's full permissions fails a state pharmacy board's audit requirement outright, and it means a bug can touch real dispensing records under an identity nobody can trace to a specific responsible person.

learningObjectives.text: Evaluate an identity/access proposal for an automation against least-privilege and individual-accountability criteria
Recognize why a shared or borrowed human login is a worse choice for an automation than a dedicated, narrowly scoped service identity

contentSections.body:
IT's first proposal for getting the intake tool talking to ScriptLedger: create a shared login, "svc-automation," and grant it the same permissions an actual working pharmacist has, so it can "do whatever it needs to do" without anyone having to figure out a narrower access scope. It's the fastest path to something working.

It's also disqualifying on its own. Corrigan & Vale operates under a state pharmacy board requirement that every action touching a dispensing record — who queued it, who filled it, who modified it — trace to a specific licensed individual. A shared automation login with full pharmacist permissions produces exactly the opposite: any action it takes shows up in ScriptLedger's logs as "svc-automation," attributable to no one, indistinguishable from every other action the same account might take. And because it holds full pharmacist-level permissions, a bug in the intake tool doesn't just produce a wrong report — it can read or alter live dispensing records with the same authority a real pharmacist has, under an identity built to have no individual accountable for it.

Identity and access for an automation is a design decision with real alternatives, not a checkbox to satisfy quickly. A **dedicated, narrowly scoped service account** — its own identity, granted only the specific permissions the automation's actual tasks require, nothing more — is the right default: it's visible and traceable as its own thing in any audit trail, and a bug in it is contained to exactly what it was actually allowed to do. A **shared or borrowed login**, human or otherwise, is worse specifically because it erases exactly the traceability an audit needs: an action taken under a shared identity can't be pinned to what caused it. Running the automation literally "as" one specific staff member's own login is worse still — it ties every automated action to one real person's professional license, so a mistake the automation makes reads, on paper, as a mistake that person made.

**Least privilege** — granting only what a task genuinely needs, read-only wherever the task allows it — isn't caution for its own sake here; it's what limits the blast radius of exactly the kind of bug this track has already spent a module on (the write-back step that makes an error real, covered later in this module). An automation that only ever needs to read yesterday's export and queue a pending request for human review doesn't need permission to modify a completed dispensing record, and shouldn't have it, regardless of how much friction that saves when scoping the access.

contentSections.intro: Specify the identity and access design for Corrigan & Vale's intake automation, the way it should go in the technical design document. Three fields.

fields.prompt: What identity should the automation run as?

options.label: a dedicated service account, distinct from any human staff login
the shared svc-automation login with full pharmacist permissions IT first proposed

feedback.dedicated-service-account: Right — a distinct, dedicated identity is what makes the automation's own actions separable from any human's in ScriptLedger's audit trail, which is the actual requirement the pharmacy board is checking for.
feedback.shared-full-perms: This is IT's original proposal, and it fails the board's individual-accountability requirement directly — any action under this login can't be traced to a specific responsible party, human or otherwise.

fields.prompt: Given the automation only needs to read yesterday's export and queue pending requests for pharmacist review, what should its write permissions cover?

options.label: only creating new pending-review entries — nothing that modifies or completes an existing dispensing record
the same full read/write access a working pharmacist has, to avoid needing to revisit the scope later

feedback.narrow-write: Right — this is least privilege applied concretely. If the task is to queue new requests for review, the automation's write access should stop exactly there, not extend to modifying records it never needs to touch.
feedback.full-access: This trades a small amount of future convenience for a permission scope that's far wider than the task requires — a bug in the automation with full pharmacist access can do far more damage than one confined to creating pending-review entries, for no benefit the automation actually uses.

fields.prompt: What should ScriptLedger's logs show for an action the automation takes?

options.label: the dedicated service account's name, clearly distinguishable from any human pharmacist or technician's own login
whichever staff member happened to be logged in when the automation ran, for simplicity

feedback.distinct-identity: Right — this is what actually satisfies "every action traces to who or what performed it." A reviewer looking at the log later can tell immediately that a given entry was automated, not guess or assume.
feedback.whoever-logged-in: This is the borrowed-login problem in a different shape — it attributes an automated action to a real person who didn't necessarily perform it, which is worse for accountability than even a shared automation login, since it actively misattributes responsibility.

contentSections.synthesis: None of these three decisions add real friction to what the automation can actually do — it still reads exports and queues pending requests exactly as designed. What they change is who or what an auditor sees responsible for each action, and how much damage a bug can do, which is the entire point of treating identity and access as a design decision rather than a setup step to get through quickly.

contentSections.title: The audit that would have found this

contentSections.body:
The pharmacy board's audit requirement isn't a hypothetical constraint invented for this lesson — it's the kind of check that finds exactly this class of shortcut, and finds it after the automation has been running for months, not during design. An auditor asking "who queued this specific pending order from March 14th" and getting back "svc-automation, which has the same permissions as a pharmacist and no individual behind it" is a finding, not a technicality — and unwinding it after the fact (reconfiguring identity, re-auditing every action the shared login took, explaining the gap to the board) costs far more than getting the identity design right before the automation goes live.

This is the same shape of problem this track's earlier module on prompt versioning addressed for a different layer: a decision that can't be traced back to exactly what produced it isn't defensible when someone asks, whether the decision was made by a prompt version nobody logged or an account nobody scoped.

An automation needs its own dedicated, narrowly scoped identity — not a shared login, and not one borrowed from a real staff member — so its actions are traceable to exactly what performed them, and a bug in it is contained to exactly what it was actually permitted to do.

title: Writing back: the step that makes it real and dangerous
description: Reading yesterday's export was harmless. Queuing a refill request directly into ScriptLedger's dispensing queue is the step where a mistake stops being a wrong report and becomes a real order a pharmacist might act on.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish an automation's read/assistive stages from its write-back stages by consequence, not by technical difficulty
Specify the extra validation, staging and rollback a write-back step needs beyond what a read-only stage requires

contentSections.title: The step where a mistake becomes real

contentSections.body:
Every stage of the intake automation built so far has been read-only or purely assistive: extracting a refill request's details from a fax or portal submission, checking it against yesterday's export, flagging anything unusual for a technician to glance at. If any of these stages gets something wrong, the result is a wrong flag or a wrong summary — annoying, but nothing has happened to a real patient yet.

The next stage is different in kind, not just in scope: taking a validated refill request and writing it into ScriptLedger's pending-dispense queue — the point at which it becomes a real order a pharmacist might pull up and fill. If the extraction stage misread a dosage from a faxed prescription and that error reaches the write-back step unchecked, the result isn't a wrong number in a report. It's an incorrect dose queued for a real patient, one step away from being dispensed by someone trusting that what's in the queue is accurate.

Every automation stage divides cleanly into two categories, and the dividing line isn't how technically hard the stage is to build — it's what happens if the stage is wrong. A **read or assistive stage** — extracting data, flagging something for review, summarizing a claim — produces a wrong report or a missed flag when it fails. Something downstream, usually a human, still has a chance to catch it before anything real happens. A **write-back stage** — anything that creates, modifies, or completes a record in the system of record — produces a real consequence when it fails, because the thing it changed is now the thing a person or process downstream will act on as if it were correct.

That difference means a write-back stage earns scrutiny the read stages don't need, in proportion to what a mistake there actually costs — not because writing is technically harder than reading, but because a mistake in it doesn't stay contained to a report. The design questions for a write-back step are correspondingly sharper: what's validated immediately before the write happens, does the written record enter in a state a human still has to actively confirm rather than one that's already live for a pharmacist to fill, and if a bad write does get through, is there a real way to find it and undo it.

contentSections.scenario: An early version of the intake tool extracts dosage from a faxed prescription image and writes it directly into ScriptLedger's pending queue as a confirmed order, tagged only with a low-confidence flag a pharmacist could optionally check. A poor-quality fax scan causes the extraction to misread "50mg" as "150mg." The order sits in the queue exactly like any other pending order, distinguishable only by a flag most technicians, busy during a dispensing rush, don't reliably check.
contentSections.question: What's the actual design flaw here — not the extraction error itself, but the step after it?

options.label: The write-back step let a low-confidence extraction enter the queue in the same state as a fully confirmed order, with review made optional rather than required before it became live
The extraction model should have been more accurate on poor-quality scans
Faxed prescriptions shouldn't be accepted as an intake channel at all

feedback.optional-review: Correct. Extraction errors on a poor scan are close to inevitable at some rate — the actual design failure is that the write-back step didn't require review before the order became indistinguishable from a fully confirmed one. A low-confidence extraction reaching the queue in the same live state as a confirmed one is the write-back step doing too little, not the extraction model doing too little.
feedback.model-accuracy: A more accurate model reduces how often this specific misread happens, but doesn't reach zero, and the design still has no real gate for the errors that remain — the fix that matters is at the write-back step, not just upstream at extraction.
feedback.no-fax: Removing fax intake would remove this specific failure's trigger, but the same design gap — low-confidence output entering the queue with only an optional flag — would eventually surface through a different channel too. The fix belongs at the write-back step, which every channel passes through.

contentSections.mechanism: The write-back step treated "low confidence" as informational rather than gating — the order became fully live in the queue regardless of confidence, with the flag as the only, easily-missed signal something needed checking. A write-back step handling the same situation correctly would hold a low-confidence order in an explicitly unconfirmed state until a human actively confirms it, rather than making confirmation something a busy technician has to remember to seek out.

contentSections.title: Staging, validation and the way back out

contentSections.body:
Once the write-back step is treated with the scrutiny its consequences deserve, three concrete design elements follow. **Validation immediately before the write** — checking the extracted dosage against the prescription's stated range, confirming the drug name matches something in Corrigan & Vale's formulary, flagging anything that doesn't pass rather than writing it anyway. **A genuinely unconfirmed state before an order is live** — not a flag on an otherwise-live order, but a distinct queue position a pharmacist has to actively move an item out of before it's fillable, so "unreviewed" is structurally different from "ready," not a label riding along on the same object. **A real rollback path** — because validation and staging reduce bad writes, they don't guarantee zero, and the design needs an answer for "a wrong order got confirmed and filled before anyone caught it" that's better than starting over from a phone call.

None of this is required at the read stages the same way. A wrong flag in a triage summary costs a technician a few minutes of unnecessary attention. A wrong order that reaches "confirmed" in the queue costs a patient a wrong medication — the asymmetry in consequence is exactly what justifies the asymmetry in how much design effort the two kinds of stage get.

A write-back step is where a mistake stops being a wrong report and becomes a real, actionable consequence — it earns validation before the write, a genuinely unconfirmed state before anything is live, and a real rollback path, in proportion to what a mistake there actually costs, not to how hard the step was to build.

title: Keeping the manual path working during rollout
description: Cutting all seven Corrigan & Vale locations over to the new intake tool on the same Monday means a single bad batch takes every location's refill process down at once — the manual path stays alive, site by site, until each one has actually proven the new one.

learningObjectives.text: Design a phased rollout that keeps a proven manual process available until a new automation has demonstrated itself at real volume
State an explicit, checkable criterion for retiring a manual fallback rather than an informal one

contentSections.body:
Corrigan & Vale's owner wants a clean story: pick a date, switch all seven locations to the new intake tool that Monday, retire the fax-and-manual-entry process everywhere at once. It's appealing precisely because it's simple to communicate to staff.

The consultant pushes back with a specific scenario: if the new tool has an undiscovered bug — a validation rule that's slightly too strict and silently drops a valid refill request, say — a single-Monday cutover means all seven locations discover it simultaneously, on the same day, with the manual process already dismantled everywhere. Patients at every location go without a refill being processed until someone notices and the fallback gets rebuilt under pressure. A phased rollout, where the manual path stays fully staffed and operational at each location until that location specifically has proven the new tool clean, means the same bug is caught at one location, on a normal day, with six others still running the tested manual process exactly as before.

A rollout plan and a design plan answer different questions, and treating "we've built and tested it" as sufficient reason to retire the old path everywhere at once conflates them. Testing proves the tool works on the cases anticipated during design. A live rollout, at real volume, at a real location, is the first time it meets everything that wasn't anticipated — an unusual fax layout, a specific insurance provider's odd formatting, a technician's workflow quirk nobody described in a discovery interview. That gap between tested and proven is exactly what a phased rollout, with the manual path still alive, is designed to absorb.

The design principle: keep the existing, proven manual process fully staffed and operational, site by site, in parallel with the new automation, until each site independently demonstrates the new one is working — not until the team is generally confident, and not on a single company-wide date chosen for how clean it sounds in an announcement.

contentSections.question: Put these steps in order for a phased rollout of Corrigan & Vale's intake tool across seven locations.
steps: Select one location to go live first, chosen for typical (not best-case) refill volume and staff mix
Run the new tool there with the manual fax/entry process still fully staffed in parallel, not as a symbolic backup
Define, in writing, the specific criterion that location must meet before its manual path can be retired
Retire that one location's manual path only once the stated criterion is actually met
Move to the next location, applying whatever was learned from the first, before repeating
contentSections.explanation: Choosing a typical rather than a best-case first location matters because a rollout that only ever gets tested at the easiest site never encounters the conditions that would actually reveal a problem. Keeping the manual path genuinely staffed — not a nominal fallback nobody's actually prepared to run — is what makes it a real safety net rather than a line in a document. A written criterion, decided in advance, is what prevents "it's been a while and it seems fine" from being the actual retirement trigger. Retiring only after the criterion is met, one location at a time, is what contains a bug's blast radius to a single site instead of all seven. Carrying lessons forward is what makes each subsequent location's phase shorter and safer than the last, rather than repeating the same discovery process seven times.

contentSections.title: A real criterion, not a vibe

contentSections.body:
"It's been running fine for a while" is not a retirement criterion — it's a feeling, and feelings drift toward optimism the longer a team has been maintaining two parallel systems and wants to stop. A real criterion is written down before rollout starts, specific enough that two different people would reach the same conclusion looking at the same data: something like two consecutive weeks with zero validation errors reaching a pharmacist unreviewed, and a technician sign-off that the volume handled matches what the location actually processes on a normal week, not a quiet one.

Whoever owns that decision should be named explicitly too — not "the team," but a specific person with the authority to say a location isn't ready yet, even under pressure to hit an announced date. The pressure to retire the manual path early is real and predictable (running two processes in parallel is genuinely more work for staff), which is exactly why the criterion needs to be decided before that pressure exists, not negotiated once it does.

Keep the proven manual path fully staffed at each location until that location specifically meets a written, decided-in-advance criterion — not a company-wide cutover date, and not a general sense that things seem to be going fine.

title: Practice — Plan Integration for Seven Awkward System Pairs
description: Seven drills, no new concepts: given a client's existing system and an automation need, apply this module's discovery-first, integration-tier, identity, write-back and rollout distinctions.

learningObjectives.text: Apply this module's integration-tier and identity/access distinctions to new client systems
Judge whether an integration plan for an awkward legacy system respects this module's write-back and rollout principles

contentSections.body: Nothing new here. Seven drills across this module's skills, ordered from where the lessons ended to one step past it. Nothing is timed, and the set doesn't expire — do all seven now or split them across a few sittings.
If a drill needed a hint, that's what to watch for in the checkpoint — not a reason to redo the set.

title: Lab — Design an Integration into a System with No API
description: Take a real or realistic legacy system with no API through this module's full discipline: its real access surface, an identity and access design, the write-back boundary with its safeguards, and a documented manual fallback.

learningObjectives.text: Map a legacy system's real access surface and match integration tiers to actual task requirements
Design identity, access, write-back safeguards and a manual fallback for an integration into a system with no API

contentSections.body: Every decision in this module got more defensible the moment it was checked against what a real legacy system actually allows, instead of what a clean design would prefer. That's the lab: pick one system with no API — real or a concretely specified plausible one — and take an automation need for it through this module's whole discipline: access surface, identity, write-back, and fallback.

contentSections.title: Your integration design for a system with no API
contentSections.brief: Pick one specific automation need that has to integrate with a real legacy system — no API, or a genuinely awkward one — from your own work, a client's, or a plausible one you can specify concretely. You're going to map what the system actually offers, design identity and access, specify the write-back boundary's safeguards, and document the failure modes and manual fallback.
contentSections.deliverable: An integration design: the system's real access surface, the integration tier chosen per need with a stated reason, an identity/access plan, the write-back stage's validation and rollback plan, and the manual fallback kept alive during rollout.

stages.title: Map the system's real access surface and identity design
stages.instructions: Name exactly what the target system offers: API (if any), scheduled exports (and their actual interval/staleness), manually-triggered exports, and nothing at all. For at least two distinct automation needs this system has to serve, match each to the integration tier that fits its actual tolerance for staleness, with a one-line reason. Then specify the identity the automation will run as, and its permission scope, applying least privilege explicitly.
stages.checkpoint: You have the system's real access surface named, at least two needs matched to a tier with a stated reason, and an identity/access plan naming a dedicated identity and its specific permission scope.

stages.title: Design the write-back boundary
stages.instructions: Identify which stage(s) of your pipeline actually write to the system of record. For each, specify what's validated immediately before the write, what a genuinely unconfirmed state looks like (not a flag on an already-live record), and a real rollback path for a bad write that already went through.
stages.checkpoint: Every write-back stage has a stated validation check, an unconfirmed-state design, and a rollback plan — not just the read/assistive stages.

stages.title: Document failure modes and the manual fallback
stages.instructions: Name at least three concrete ways this integration could fail in production (a schema/screen-layout change, an export that doesn't run, a write that reaches a bad state) and what should happen when each does. Then specify the manual fallback: what it is, who runs it, and the explicit, written criterion for when it can be retired at a given site — not a vague sense of confidence.
stages.checkpoint: You have at least three named failure modes with a stated response each, and a manual fallback with an explicit retirement criterion.

rubric.criterion: The system's real access surface is stated concretely, not assumed
rubric.meets: A reader unfamiliar with the system could name exactly what API, export, or manual-trigger access actually exists, confirmed rather than guessed.

rubric.criterion: Integration tier choices are matched to actual staleness tolerance, with a reason
rubric.meets: Each need names why its chosen tier (API, export, or none) fits how much delay that specific need can tolerate.

rubric.criterion: Identity and access follow least privilege and individual accountability
rubric.meets: A dedicated identity is named, distinct from any shared or human login, with a permission scope limited to what the automation's tasks actually require.

rubric.criterion: Every write-back stage has validation, an unconfirmed state, and a rollback plan
rubric.meets: No write-back stage relies on an optional flag on an already-live record as its only safeguard.

rubric.criterion: Failure modes are specific and each has a stated response
rubric.meets: At least three failure modes are named concretely (not 'something could go wrong'), each with what should happen when it does.

rubric.criterion: The manual fallback has an explicit, written retirement criterion
rubric.meets: The criterion is specific enough that two different people would reach the same conclusion from the same data — not a general sense that things seem fine.

contentSections.body: An integration design tested against what the system actually allows — not what a clean architecture would prefer — is the only version of the design you're entitled to hand to a client.

title: Checkpoint — Integration and the Systems Already There
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from three modules back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's integration distinctions, and earlier modules' prompt-as-spec and tool-selection distinctions, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Integration and the Systems Already There

questions.from: This module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: A consultant sketches an architecture assuming ScriptLedger has a live API, before any discovery session confirms it. What was the actual mistake?

options.label: Designing around an assumption about the target system instead of a confirmed fact, discovered before drawing anything
Choosing to design an architecture at all before pricing the engagement
Using a diagram instead of written prose to describe the design

questions.explanation: The existing systems set the actual boundary of what's buildable — treating that as confirmed before design starts, rather than assumed from how comparable systems usually work, is the whole discipline this module opens with.

questions.from: This module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: Why was ScriptLedger's nightly export a poor fit for the same-day double-dispense check, even though it was a perfectly good fit for the weekly owner report?

options.label: The double-dispense check needs to know about something filled earlier today, which a source that's always at least a day stale structurally can't show
The weekly report requires more data volume than the export could provide
Nightly exports are unreliable in general and shouldn't be used for anything

questions.explanation: The right integration tier depends on how much delay a specific task can tolerate. A weekly report has no same-day requirement at all; a same-day double-dispense check does, which the always-a-day-stale export structurally cannot satisfy.

questions.from: This module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: Why did running the intake automation under a shared "svc-automation" login with full pharmacist permissions fail the pharmacy board's audit requirement?

options.label: Every action needs to trace to a specific licensed individual, and a shared login with broad permissions makes an action untraceable to what actually caused it
Shared logins are always technically slower than dedicated ones
The pharmacy board doesn't allow any automation to touch dispensing records under any circumstances

questions.explanation: The board's requirement was specifically about individual accountability — a shared login with full permissions and no dedicated identity produces actions that can't be pinned to what performed them, and grants far more access than least privilege would allow.

questions.from: This module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: What made the write-back step of queuing a refill request more dangerous than the earlier extraction and flagging stages, even though all three could contain the same kind of error?

options.label: A mistake at the write-back stage becomes a real, actionable order a pharmacist might fill, while a mistake at a read/flagging stage produces a wrong report a human still has a chance to catch
The write-back stage was technically more difficult to build correctly
Write-back stages always require more code than read stages

questions.explanation: The distinction this module draws is about consequence, not difficulty — a write-back stage changes the system of record itself, so an error there is one step from becoming a real action, unlike an error in a stage that only produces a report or a flag.

questions.from: Previous module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: Per the previous module, why did Aldermere's "friendlier tone" prompt edit — swapping "homeowner" for "policyholder" — cause real claims to go unflagged, even though it wasn't meant to touch classification logic at all?

options.label: The swapped word had been functioning as an incidental urgency pattern-match cue in the few-shot examples, so removing it shifted classification for a whole category of claims
The new wording was factually incorrect about who the claimant was
The edit made the prompt too long to process correctly

questions.explanation: The prompt is the business logic — a wording change in the examples can shift what the model pattern-matches to, even when the change looks purely cosmetic, which is exactly why the previous module treats any wording edit as needing the same review a code change would get.

questions.from: Previous module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: Why did Aldermere's routing script silently misroute a genuinely urgent claim when the model described it as needing attention "fairly soon" instead of "urgent"?

options.label: The routing script was searching free-text prose for specific keywords instead of reading a defined, enumerated field the model had been asked to set directly
The model was wrong about the claim's actual urgency
The claim was missing required information

questions.explanation: The model correctly judged the claim urgent — the failure was structural: recovering a decision from prose by keyword search breaks the moment phrasing drifts, which is exactly why the previous module's fix was a closed enumerated field the routing code reads directly.

questions.from: Previous module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: Why did testing a prompt revision only against the three multi-peril claims it was meant to fix fail to catch the new error it introduced on routine plumbing-mention claims?

options.label: A test set that only contains the target case can only confirm the target case improved — it has no unrelated cases in it to reveal a side effect outside its own scope
Three test cases is always too small a sample size for any test
The plumbing-mention claims were mislabeled in the gold set

questions.explanation: This is the structural point of the regression-testing lesson: a narrow test set, by construction, cannot detect a side effect that falls outside what it contains — only a full gold-set comparison surfaced the new plumbing-claim error.

questions.from: Previous module — Prompts as Production Components
questions.prompt: Why couldn't Aldermere answer a regulator's question about exactly what criteria classified a specific claim from six months earlier?

options.label: The prompt had been edited four times since with no saved version history, so there was no way to reconstruct which version actually produced that decision
The regulator's question was outside the scope of what any insurer is required to answer
The claim itself had been deleted from Aldermere's records

questions.explanation: Without a version-tagged, immutably stored copy of each shipped prompt and a log connecting each decision to the exact version that made it, a past decision can't be reconstructed or defended months later — the exact gap the previous module's versioning lesson addresses.

questions.from: Three modules back — Choosing Tools You Can Defend
questions.prompt: Per the tool-selection module, why did Halsted's analyst's free weekend-build script end up costing three weeks of silent wrong extractions?

options.label: The plan had no named owner and no drift detection for when a broker's template changed, so nobody was positioned to notice when it started failing
Python was an inappropriate language for the task
The script ran too slowly to keep up with claim volume

questions.explanation: The build wasn't the wrong technical choice — it was scoped only to current templates with nobody assigned to notice or fix a template change, an unassigned maintenance cost that's exactly as real as a budgeted one, just unpredictable in when it lands.

questions.from: Three modules back — Choosing Tools You Can Defend
questions.prompt: What did a vendor contract's proprietary-assets clause actually mean for Halsted, even though the same contract said raw data exports cleanly on termination?

options.label: The field-mapping and exception-rule configuration Halsted built up over time wouldn't travel, meaning leaving the vendor meant rebuilding that tuning from zero
Halsted would legally own none of its own claims data
The clause had no real effect, since the data itself was portable

questions.explanation: The reassuring data-export clause hid the actual dependency in a separate clause — months of configuration work don't travel with a clean data export, which is real, underestimated exit cost that a clean data-portability answer can mask.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.

title: The automation nobody can maintain is a liability
description: Eleven days of silently piling-up refill requests at Corrigan & Vale didn't happen because the automation broke in a hard way — it happened because nobody at the client knew it existed as a discrete thing with an owner, so nobody knew who to call.

learningObjectives.text: Explain why an automation only the consultant understands is a liability independent of how well it was built
Recognize the difference between a deliverable that works and a deliverable someone else can keep working

contentSections.body:
Six months after the intake automation went live across all seven Corrigan & Vale locations — the consultant who built it long gone, the engagement closed out cleanly, the invoice paid — the fax-to-email gateway vendor changes their webhook format in a routine update. The automation, which depended on that exact format to receive new refill requests, stops receiving anything. No error message reaches anyone; from the gateway's side, the update succeeded and everything looks fine.

Nobody at Corrigan & Vale knows the automation exists as a discrete system with its own dependencies — it was described to staff during rollout as "the new refill process," not as a specific piece of software with a specific vendor integration that could specifically break. Refill requests silently stop being triaged. It takes eleven days for a pharmacist, doing an unrelated manual spot-check, to notice a backlog that shouldn't exist and start asking why. Nobody she asks knows who originally built the system, whether it's supposed to be monitored, or who to call.

The automation itself did nothing wrong in a technical sense — a vendor changing a webhook format without warning is a real, foreseeable kind of external change, and no design perfectly immune to it exists. What actually failed was something upstream of the code: nobody at Corrigan & Vale understood the automation well enough to know it could break this way, notice when it had, or know who to call about it. The system worked exactly as built for as long as its environment stayed the same, and the moment it didn't, the client had no way to respond.

This is the failure mode this whole module is built around. A deliverable that works at handover and a deliverable the client can keep working are different things, and a consulting engagement that only produces the first has produced a liability with a delay on it — not a finished project, a countdown to the day something changes and nobody notices. The lessons that follow are the specific practices that turn "it works" into "they can run it without me": a runbook, monitoring that makes failure loud, training aimed at the right person, and a real off switch.

contentSections.scenario: Two different consultants finish similar automation engagements the same month. Consultant A hands over clean, well-commented code and a technical architecture diagram, and answers questions for two weeks after launch before going fully unavailable. Consultant B hands over the same code, plus a plain-language runbook naming who owns the system, what it depends on, how to tell if it's broken, and who's allowed to turn it off — and trains the actual technicians who'll run it day to day, not just the owner who bought the project.
contentSections.question: Which consultant actually left the client able to run the system without them, and why?

options.label: Consultant A — clean code and a real architecture diagram is the technically complete deliverable
Consultant B — the runbook, named ownership, and training aimed at the actual operators is what lets the client detect and respond to a problem without calling the consultant
Both equally — two weeks of availability after launch covers the same gap either way

feedback.consultant-a: Clean code is necessary but not sufficient — code a client's technicians can't read, with no plain-language explanation of what depends on what or who's responsible for noticing a failure, leaves them exactly where Corrigan & Vale was: unable to tell something's wrong, let alone fix it.
feedback.consultant-b: Right. The difference isn't code quality — it's whether the people who'll actually encounter a problem know the system exists, know what it depends on, know it's supposed to be watched, and know who's allowed to act. That's what "they can run it without me" actually requires.
feedback.both-equal: Two weeks of consultant availability after launch is a bridge, not a handover — it delays the moment the client is on their own without addressing whether they'll be ready for that moment when it comes six months later, which is exactly when Corrigan & Vale's gateway change happened.

contentSections.concept: An automation nobody can maintain is a liability regardless of how well it was built — the deliverable this module is about isn't the working code, it's the client's ability to notice, understand and respond to that code the day something changes.

contentSections.title: What handover actually has to answer

contentSections.body:
A useful test for whether a handover is real: pick a plausible failure — a vendor changing a format, a dependency going down, an unusual input the system wasn't built for — and ask whether a named person at the client, today, without calling the consultant, could notice it happened, understand roughly why, and know what to do next. If the honest answer is "no, they'd have to call whoever built it," the handover isn't finished, whatever the contract says was delivered.

This isn't a standard every engagement can meet perfectly — some failures genuinely need the original builder's judgment. But most of what actually breaks in production is mundane and repeats a pattern (a format change, an expired credential, an unusual volume spike), and mundane, repeating failures are exactly the ones a runbook and the right training can prepare someone for. The rest of this module is about which specific practices close that gap.

contentSections.code:
Corrigan & Vale's project close-out email, sent at the end of the engagement:

"The intake automation is now live at all seven locations. Documentation and code are in the shared drive. Please reach out with any questions. Thanks for a great project!"
contentSections.question: What's missing from this close-out that the eleven-day silent failure exposed?

options.label: No named owner, no description of what the system depends on, and no statement of who's supposed to notice if it stops working
The email should have included a more detailed technical architecture diagram
The email should have been sent to more people at Corrigan & Vale

feedback.no-ownership-monitoring: Correct. "Documentation is in the shared drive" isn't the same as someone at the client knowing what that documentation says, being responsible for checking on the system, or knowing they're responsible before something goes wrong. This close-out transferred files, not the ability to operate the system.
feedback.more-diagram: A more detailed architecture diagram helps someone who's already looking for a problem understand it faster — it doesn't help anyone know to look in the first place, which was the actual gap that let eleven days pass.
feedback.more-recipients: More recipients on the same generic email doesn't create a named, accountable owner — it diffuses responsibility across a group rather than assigning it to someone specific, which tends to produce the same outcome as assigning it to no one.

contentSections.flawExplanation: A close-out that hands over files and an open invitation to "reach out with questions" assumes the client will know when to ask a question — but the whole point of a silent failure is that nothing prompts anyone to ask. What was missing wasn't more documentation; it was a named owner, a description of what the system depends on, and an explicit answer to "who's supposed to notice if this breaks," none of which a shared drive full of files provides on its own.

contentSections.body: An automation only the consultant understands is a liability with a delay on it, not a finished deliverable — the actual test of a handover is whether a named person at the client could notice, understand, and respond to a plausible failure without calling the consultant.

title: Runbooks written for the person who wasn't in the meetings
description: "Check the queue" and "restart the intake step" mean nothing to a pharmacy technician who's never seen the build process — a real runbook names the exact login, the exact screen, and the exact click, for someone with zero shared context.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a runbook entry usable by someone with zero project context from notes that assume shared context
Write a runbook entry for a specific named failure mode, covering symptom, check, action and escalation

contentSections.title: Notes that only make sense to the person who wrote them

contentSections.body:
Rebuilding the intake automation's documentation after the eleven-day outage, the new consultant finds the original build notes: "If the queue looks stuck, check the intake step's logs and restart the poller if the last successful run is stale." Perfectly clear to whoever wrote it, mid-build, with the whole system's architecture fresh in their head.

To Marisol, the pharmacy technician who's now nominally responsible for the system and has never seen its source code, every phrase in that sentence is a locked door: which queue, looks stuck how, where are "the intake step's logs," what counts as stale, what does "restart the poller" even mean or where would she click to do it. The note isn't wrong — it's written for a reader who doesn't exist anymore, someone who was in the room while the system was being built. Marisol, reading it cold six months later with a genuine backlog in front of her, gets nothing usable out of it.

A runbook entry is written for the reader with the least context who will plausibly need it — not the consultant six months from now, and not a future engineer who happens to inherit the codebase, but whoever is actually on shift when something goes wrong, which at Corrigan & Vale means a pharmacy technician with no software background at all. That reframes what "clear documentation" means: not technically accurate, but usable cold, by someone who wasn't in any of the meetings where the system's internals were discussed.

A real entry for one named failure mode has four parts, each answering a question the technical build notes above skip entirely. **What it looks like** — the concrete, observable symptom a non-technical person would actually notice ("no new refill requests have appeared in the queue for over two hours," not "the poller has stopped"). **Where to check** — the literal screen, login, and location, named exactly, not "the logs" as if that's self-explanatory. **What to do** — the specific action, in the order to take it, written as steps a first-time reader could follow without guessing. **Who to call if that doesn't fix it** — a real name or role, not "IT," and what information to have ready when they do.

contentSections.problem: Turn this technical build note into a runbook entry Marisol could actually use: "If the queue looks stuck, check the intake step's logs and restart the poller if the last successful run is stale."
