steps.label: Translate the symptom into something a non-technical reader would actually observe
steps.work: "No new refill requests have appeared in the pending-review queue for more than two hours during business hours" — replacing "looks stuck" with a concrete, checkable observation.
steps.why: "Looks stuck" assumes the reader already knows what normal looks like well enough to spot abnormal. A specific, time-bound symptom is checkable by someone seeing the system for the first time.

steps.label: Name the exact place to check, not the category of place
steps.work: "Open the Intake Monitor tab in the admin dashboard (login: admin portal, top-right menu → Intake Monitor). The 'Last successful check' timestamp should update every 15 minutes during business hours."
steps.why: "Check the logs" assumes the reader knows what logs are, where they live, and how to read them. A named tab, a named login location, and a stated normal-behavior baseline turn a vague direction into something followable.

steps.label: Give the action as literal steps, not a technical instruction
steps.work: "1. If the timestamp is more than 30 minutes old, click 'Restart Intake Service' in the same tab. 2. Wait 5 minutes and refresh. 3. If the timestamp updates, the fix worked — check the queue again in 30 minutes to confirm requests are flowing."
steps.why: "Restart the poller" is a phrase from the codebase, not an instruction. Numbered, literal steps — click this, wait this long, check this — are what someone with zero technical background can actually execute under pressure.

faded.problem: The runbook also needs an entry for what happens if the restart in step 1 above doesn't fix it — the timestamp stays stale after two attempts.

blanks.prompt: What should the entry say to do, given the simple fix didn't work?
blanks.answer: Escalate to a named person or role, with specific information to include (e.g. the timestamp, what was already tried, since when)
accept: call the named contact with details
blanks.why: A runbook that dead-ends at 'if that doesn't work, something is wrong' leaves the reader stuck exactly where they started. A real escalation path names who to contact and what to tell them, so the next person doesn't have to reconstruct what was already tried.

blanks.prompt: Why does the escalation step need to name a specific person or role, not just "contact support"?
blanks.answer: "Contact support" is exactly the kind of vague direction that failed Corrigan & Vale for eleven days — nobody knew who to call
accept: it repeats the original failure of nobody knowing who to call
vague escalation is what caused the 11-day gap
blanks.why: This is the same gap that let the original outage run for eleven days: nobody at Corrigan & Vale knew who was responsible. A runbook that reintroduces "contact support" as its own escalation path hasn't actually closed that gap, just moved it one step later.

contentSections.procedure: Every runbook entry translates a technical symptom into an observable one, names the exact place to check (not the category), gives literal numbered steps for the fix, and ends with a named escalation contact and what information to bring them — written throughout for a reader who wasn't in any of the build meetings.

contentSections.body:
A runbook doesn't need an entry for every conceivable failure — that's an infinite, unwritable list, and a hundred-page document nobody reads under pressure fails the same usability test as no document at all. It needs entries for the failure modes that are actually plausible and actually recurring: the ones this module's next lesson on monitoring is built to detect, and the ones a genuinely careful discovery process (the same kind covered in the previous module, applied to "what tends to break") can name in advance.

A practical starting list for most automations: the data source stops updating (Corrigan & Vale's actual failure), a downstream write starts failing or returning unexpected errors, volume spikes past what the system was sized for, and a credential or connection expires. Four or five well-written entries covering the failures that are actually likely beat twenty shallow entries covering everything anyone could imagine — the same "genuine, checkable specifics over exhaustive vagueness" principle this track has applied to risk registers and validation gold sets elsewhere.

A runbook entry is written for the reader with the least context who will plausibly need it — the exact observable symptom, the exact place to check, literal numbered steps, and a named person to escalate to, for a short list of failures that are actually likely, not an exhaustive one nobody will read.

title: Making it obvious when it stops working
description: Eleven days passed because nothing watched for "zero new intake records in a stretch of business hours" — a cheap, simple check nobody built, and the specific gap that let a mundane vendor change turn into eleven days of unprocessed refills.

learningObjectives.text: Design a cheap, targeted monitoring check for a specific known failure mode rather than generic system health monitoring
Route an alert to someone positioned and expected to act on it, avoiding both silence and alert fatigue

contentSections.body:
Rebuilding the intake system after the eleven-day outage, the new consultant asks a simple question: what would have caught this in hours instead of days? The answer turns out to be almost embarrassingly cheap — a check that runs every hour during business hours and asks one question: has at least one new refill request appeared in the intake queue in the last two hours? Corrigan & Vale processes refills steadily enough throughout the day that two hours with zero new intake, during business hours, is itself the signal something's wrong, regardless of what the underlying cause turns out to be.

Nobody built this check the first time, because nothing about it felt like part of "the automation" — it wasn't a feature the client asked for, and building the intake pipeline itself felt like the whole job. But it's exactly the kind of check that would have turned the vendor's webhook format change from an eleven-day silent failure into a same-morning alert, without needing to predict that specific vendor change in advance at all.

Effective monitoring for a handed-over automation isn't generic system health monitoring — CPU usage, uptime percentages, the kind of dashboard built for an engineering team watching infrastructure. It's a small number of targeted checks, each built around a specific, plausible failure symptom, cheap enough that "why didn't we just build this" is the honest reaction once it's pointed out. "Has expected activity happened in the expected window" — new requests arriving, a scheduled export actually running, a write actually landing — catches an entire category of failures (upstream dependency breaks, silent stalls, format changes) without needing to know in advance exactly what broke, only that something did.

The check doesn't need to diagnose the cause. It needs to make the absence of normal activity visible to a person, quickly, instead of leaving it undiscovered until someone happens to notice a backlog by hand — which is the entire gap that turned a routine vendor update into eleven silent days.

contentSections.scenario: Before this check existed, Corrigan & Vale's intake automation ran silently broken for eleven full days before a pharmacist's manual spot-check happened to catch it.
contentSections.question: Once the hourly "zero new intake in two business hours" check is running and alerting a named person, roughly how long would you expect the same underlying failure (a silent stop in new intake) to go undetected?
contentSections.explanation: With the check running hourly and alerting on a two-hour gap during business hours, the same failure is caught within roughly two hours instead of eleven days — a difference of almost 130x, achieved by one cheap, targeted check rather than by predicting the specific vendor change in advance. The number matters less than the mechanism: a check built around "is expected activity happening," not around guessing the exact cause, catches an entire category of otherwise-silent failures.

contentSections.body:
A check that fires is only useful if it reaches someone positioned and expected to act on it — and the two failure modes on either side of that are both real. Alerting no one, or alerting an inbox nobody's assigned to watch, reproduces exactly the eleven-day gap with extra steps: a check existed, it just didn't reach anyone. Alerting too much — a check so sensitive it fires on ordinary, harmless variation, several times a week — teaches whoever receives it to stop looking closely, the same automation-bias pattern this track covered for human review of AI outputs: a signal that's usually noise gets ignored, including the one time it isn't.

The fix on both sides is specific, not generic: name exactly who receives the alert (a role with clear ownership, like "the on-duty pharmacy manager," not an unmonitored shared inbox), and calibrate the check's sensitivity against real historical data — Corrigan & Vale's two-hour threshold came from knowing the location's actual typical gap between refill requests during business hours, not a round number picked without checking.

contentSections.scenario: Designing the alert routing for the new intake-monitoring check. Some choices genuinely reduce the risk of a repeat of the eleven-day gap. Some sound like they help but don't.
contentSections.question: Select every choice that actually reduces the risk of either silence or alert fatigue.

items.label: The alert goes to "the on-duty pharmacy manager" — a role with a specific, always-staffed person behind it, not a shared inbox
The two-hour threshold was set by checking six months of historical intake timing, not chosen as a round number
The alert is also CC'd to the entire corporate email list, "just in case," so more people are aware
If the manager doesn't acknowledge the alert within 30 minutes, it automatically escalates to a second named contact
The threshold is set to 15 minutes instead of two hours, to catch problems "as early as possible"
Alerts are written to a log file that's reviewed during the weekly team meeting

explanation.named-role: Applicable. A specific, always-staffed role is exactly what closes the "nobody knew who to call" gap from the original outage — it's the alerting equivalent of the runbook's named escalation contact.
explanation.threshold-from-data: Applicable. A threshold grounded in the location's actual historical pattern is what makes the check sensitive to real problems without firing constantly on ordinary variation — an un-researched round number risks either extreme.
explanation.everyone-gets-it: Not applicable, and it's a version of the alert-fatigue problem: an alert everyone gets is functionally an alert no one owns, since no single person is accountable for acting on it — closer to the shared-inbox failure than it looks.
explanation.escalation-path: Applicable. This is what prevents a single missed alert (the manager is out sick, in a meeting) from silently becoming another multi-day gap — the same logic as a runbook's escalation step for when the first fix doesn't work.
explanation.lower-threshold: Not applicable, and this is the alert-fatigue trap specifically. If Corrigan & Vale's actual normal gap between requests during a slow hour is sometimes 15-20 minutes, a 15-minute threshold fires constantly on harmless variation, training whoever receives it to stop looking closely — exactly the failure mode this module warns against.
explanation.silent-log: Not applicable. A log reviewed once a week is functionally the same as no alert at all for anything time-sensitive — it would have caught the eleven-day outage on roughly the same multi-day timescale it actually took, just with extra structure around the delay.

contentSections.synthesis: The choices that help share a pattern: a specific, accountable person receives the alert, the threshold is grounded in real data rather than intuition, and there's a real path for when the first person doesn't respond. The choices that don't help share the opposite pattern: broadening "who's aware" without narrowing "who's accountable," and tightening sensitivity without checking it against what's actually normal — both of which look like they're making the system safer while actually reproducing a version of the original gap.

contentSections.body: A cheap, targeted check for whether expected activity is happening — not generic system health monitoring — catches an entire category of silent failures without needing to predict the specific cause, but only if it alerts a specific, accountable person at a threshold calibrated against real data, with a real escalation path for when that person doesn't respond.

title: Training the operator, not the sponsor
description: The training session went to the owner who bought the project, who nodded along in the demo and forgot everything by the following week — the technicians who'd actually run day-to-day triage were never invited at all.

learningObjectives.text: Identify the actual day-to-day operator of a system as distinct from its sponsor or buyer
Design hands-on training using real scenarios aimed at the operator's actual day-to-day decisions

contentSections.title: The training the wrong person got

contentSections.body:
The original intake automation's launch training was a one-hour video call with Corrigan & Vale's owner — the person who signed the contract, sat in the kickoff meetings, and cared about the project's ROI. The consultant walked through a polished demo: here's how a request comes in, here's how it gets triaged, here's the dashboard. The owner nodded, asked a couple of high-level questions about volume projections, and thanked the consultant for a smooth rollout.

The pharmacy technicians at all seven locations — the people who would actually see a triaged request appear on their screen every single day, decide what to do when something looked wrong, and be the first to notice if the queue stopped moving — were never in that call. Nobody scheduled a session with them at all; the assumption was that the owner would "roll it out" to the team. By the time Marisol needed to know what to do about a stuck queue, the one training session that had happened was six months gone, delivered to someone who was never going to be the one troubleshooting it.

The person who buys an automation and the person who runs it day to day are very often different people, and a training plan aimed at whichever one is in the room during the sales and kickoff conversations — usually the sponsor — misses the one who actually needs it. The sponsor needs to understand the system well enough to trust it and champion it; the operator needs to understand it well enough to work inside it every day, including the days something's slightly off. Those are different kinds of understanding, and a single polished demo aimed at the sponsor's questions (ROI, timeline, headline capability) answers neither of the operator's real questions: what do I do when this specific thing happens, and how do I tell if something's wrong.

Identifying the real operator sometimes takes a genuine question, not an assumption — at Corrigan & Vale it's the pharmacy technicians, not the pharmacy owner; at a different client it might be a single admin coordinator, or a rotating on-call team, or, awkwardly, nobody currently employed in a role that would naturally own it, which is itself a finding worth surfacing before handover rather than after.

contentSections.scenario: A different automation engagement: an inventory-reconciliation tool built for a mid-size retailer. The consultant delivers a one-hour training session to the operations director who commissioned the project, covering the system's capabilities and its dashboard. Three months later, the warehouse staff who actually run daily reconciliation are still doing it manually, unaware the tool exists, because nobody trained them and the operations director assumed IT would "roll it out" eventually.
contentSections.question: What's the actual mechanism behind the tool sitting unused three months later?

options.label: Training was delivered to the sponsor who commissioned the project, not to the operators who would actually use it day to day, and nobody explicitly owned getting it to them
The tool was too complicated for warehouse staff to learn
The operations director didn't care about the project's success

feedback.wrong-audience: Correct. This is the same gap as Corrigan & Vale's pharmacy owner training — the person in the room for the sales and kickoff process isn't automatically the person who needs hands-on training, and "IT will roll it out eventually" is exactly the kind of assumption that leaves the actual operators untrained indefinitely, with nobody specifically responsible for closing that gap.
feedback.too-complex: There's no evidence the tool itself was too complex — the warehouse staff never got any training on it at all, so their difficulty (if any) with the tool's complexity was never actually tested.
feedback.didnt-care: The operations director's motivation isn't the mechanism here — a caring sponsor and an indifferent one produce the same outcome if the training plan itself never named who the actual operators were and put a session directly in front of them.

contentSections.mechanism: A training plan built around the people present during the sales and kickoff process defaults to the sponsor, because the sponsor is who's in the room. Reaching the actual operators requires deliberately identifying them as a distinct audience and scheduling training specifically for them — an omission that produces the identical unused-tool outcome whether the sponsor is engaged and well-meaning or not, because the gap is structural, not motivational.

contentSections.title: Training that survives contact with a real day

contentSections.body:
A demo — here's how the happy path works, click by click — is the wrong shape for operator training even when it's aimed at the right audience. A demo shows the system working; an operator's actual job is mostly deciding what to do on the days it doesn't look quite right. Effective training for the technicians at Corrigan & Vale would walk through real, specific scenarios from the runbook built earlier in this module: here's what a stuck queue looks like, here's exactly where you'd check, here's what you'd click, here's who you'd call if that doesn't fix it — hands-on, with the actual interface, not narrated over a slide.

The best evidence a training session worked isn't a nodding head on a video call — it's the operator successfully handling a walked-through version of a real scenario themselves, with the trainer watching rather than driving. If Marisol can work through "the queue hasn't updated in two hours" using the actual dashboard during training, with the runbook in front of her, that's a much stronger signal than any amount of head-nodding during a polished demo.

Identify the actual day-to-day operator — often not the person who bought the project — and train them hands-on against real runbook scenarios using the real interface, not a polished demo delivered to whoever was in the sales and kickoff meetings.

title: The off switch, and who is allowed to use it
description: An update breaks something at Corrigan & Vale and the on-site pharmacist has no documented way to stop the automation and fall back to manual entry without calling the consultant at 9pm — every handover needs a real, low-friction off switch and a named person allowed to use it.

learningObjectives.text: Specify a genuine, low-friction off switch and fallback path as part of a handover, not an afterthought
Name explicit authority for who can invoke the off switch without needing the original builder's permission

contentSections.title: The 9pm phone call that shouldn't have been necessary

contentSections.body:
A minor update to Corrigan & Vale's intake system — pushed by the (new) consultant maintaining it, meant to fix an unrelated bug — introduces a regression that causes the write-back step to occasionally queue a refill under the wrong patient's name. It's caught fast, within the hour, by an alert from the monitoring built earlier in this module. But then nothing happens for twenty minutes, because the on-site pharmacist at the location where it's happening has no way to stop the automation herself. There's no documented off switch, no button, no fallback instruction — just a phone number for the consultant, who doesn't pick up until she calls a second time.

The manual fax-and-entry path from the module on integration was retired at this location months ago, once it met its rollout criterion — correctly, at the time. But retiring the manual path and failing to leave behind a way to temporarily fall back to it under a known-bad-automation scenario are two different decisions, and only the first one was made deliberately.

Every handover needs a genuine, low-friction way to turn the automation off and fall back to a known-working alternative — and "genuine" and "low-friction" both matter. A theoretical off switch that requires calling the original consultant isn't a fallback the client can use without the consultant, which defeats the entire purpose of this module. A real one is something the client can execute themselves, documented in the same plain-language style as the runbook: what "off" actually means for this system (does new intake stop, does the existing queue stay accessible, does it revert to accepting requests by fax), exactly how to trigger it, and what the fallback process looks like once it's off.

That fallback doesn't have to mean keeping the full manual process staffed forever — the previous module's rollout discipline was right to retire it once it was proven redundant. It does mean the handover needs an explicit, documented answer for "what do we do for the next few hours or days if the automation needs to be off," even after the training-wheels manual path is gone, which might be a lighter, temporary version of the old process rather than the exact thing that used to run in parallel.

contentSections.intro: Specify the off switch for Corrigan & Vale's intake automation the way it should appear in the handover pack. Four fields.

fields.prompt: What should "off" concretely do to the system?

options.label: stop accepting and processing new intake, while keeping the existing queue and its history visible and accessible
delete all pending and historical records so there's a clean slate to restart from later

feedback.stop-new-keep-visible: Right — this stops the specific problem (new, potentially bad writes) without destroying anything a pharmacist might still need to see or act on from before the switch was flipped.
feedback.delete-everything: This would make an already-bad situation worse — deleting records during an active incident destroys exactly the information (what was already queued, what might need correcting) that's most needed while the problem is being sorted out.

fields.prompt: Who should be explicitly authorized to trigger the off switch?

options.label: a named on-site role at each location (e.g. the on-duty pharmacist), documented in advance, not requiring anyone's real-time permission
only the consultant or vendor who built the system, contacted in real time for each use

feedback.named-on-site-role: Right — this is what actually would have prevented the twenty-minute delay. Authority decided and documented in advance means the person facing the problem doesn't need anyone's live permission to act.
feedback.consultant-only: This is exactly the gap the hook describes — an off switch that requires the consultant's real-time involvement to use isn't a fallback the client can execute without the consultant, defeating the purpose of building one at all.

fields.prompt: How should the trigger itself be documented?

options.label: a specific, named action in the runbook's plain-language style — exact screen, exact button, exact confirmation step
a general instruction to "disable the automation" using whatever method seems appropriate at the time

feedback.specific-documented-action: Right — this follows the same discipline as the earlier runbook lesson: a vague instruction is unusable to someone reading it for the first time under pressure, exactly when they'd need to use it.
feedback.vague-instruction: "Whatever method seems appropriate" asks someone in an active incident to improvise a shutdown procedure they've never used before, which is precisely the situation a documented, specific action exists to prevent.

fields.prompt: What should the handover pack say happens to incoming refill requests once the automation is off?

options.label: a documented, if lighter, temporary process for handling requests manually until the automation is back on — not left unanswered
nothing specific — the location can figure out a temporary process once they actually need one

feedback.documented-temp-fallback: Right — turning the automation off without an answer for what handles incoming requests in the meantime just trades one problem (a bad automated write) for another (no way to process refills at all).
feedback.figure-it-out-later: This leaves a location that's just discovered a serious problem to also invent a manual process from scratch, under pressure, at the worst possible moment to be improvising — exactly what a documented handover is supposed to prevent.

contentSections.synthesis: Together, these four decisions turn "there should be an off switch" into something a specific, named, already-authorized person can actually execute during a real incident, without waiting on a phone call that might not be answered — which is the entire point of a handover, applied to the one moment a client is most likely to need it and least likely to have the patience to improvise.

contentSections.title: Documented authority, decided before it's needed

contentSections.body:
The reason authority has to be decided and written down in advance, not figured out in the moment, is the same reason the previous module insisted a rollout's retirement criterion be written before the pressure to retire early existed: a decision made calmly, ahead of time, is more reliable than the same decision made under the stress of an actual incident, when the instinct to defer to whoever built the system (even if they're unreachable) is strongest exactly when it's least useful.

This closes the loop the whole module has been building toward. A runbook that names what to check and do; monitoring that makes a problem visible fast; training that makes the operator capable of acting on what the runbook says; and an off switch that same operator is explicitly authorized to use, without permission, the moment they need to — together, these are what "they can run it without me" actually means, tested against the worst case, not the best one.

A real off switch is documented, specific, and usable by a named person authorized in advance — not something that requires calling the original consultant — with a real answer for what happens to incoming work while it's off, decided before an incident, not during one.

title: Lab — Write the Complete Handover Pack for an Automation
description: Take a real or realistic automation through this module's full discipline: a runbook covering its likely failures, a monitoring plan, an identified and trained operator, and a documented off switch with named authority.

learningObjectives.text: Write runbook entries usable by a reader with zero project context, for a system's actually likely failure modes
Specify monitoring, an operator training plan, and a genuine off switch as a complete, coherent handover pack

contentSections.body: Every practice in this module got real the moment it was tested against a reader who wasn't in the room when the system was built. That's the lab: pick one automation — from your own work, a client's, or a plausible one you can specify concretely — and produce the complete handover pack a client would actually need to run it without you.

contentSections.title: Your complete handover pack
contentSections.brief: Pick one specific automation — real or a concretely specified plausible one. You're going to name its actual operator, write runbook entries for its most likely failure modes, specify a monitoring plan that would catch those failures fast, and document a genuine off switch with named authority to use it.
contentSections.deliverable: A handover pack: the named operator and how they were identified, 3-4 runbook entries for likely failure modes, a monitoring plan naming what's checked and who's alerted, and an off-switch specification with pre-authorized ownership and a fallback for incoming work.

stages.title: Name the operator and the likely failure modes
stages.instructions: Identify who actually operates this system day to day — by role or name, not by assumption — and how you'd confirm that if you weren't sure. Then name 3-4 concrete, plausible, recurring failure modes for this specific system (not a generic list), the kind a runbook and monitoring should actually be built around.
stages.checkpoint: You have a named operator with a stated reason it's them and not the sponsor, and 3-4 specific failure modes grounded in what this particular system actually depends on.

stages.title: Write the runbook entries
stages.instructions: For each failure mode from stage 1, write a full runbook entry: the concrete observable symptom, the exact place to check, literal numbered steps for the fix, and a named escalation contact with what information to bring them.
stages.checkpoint: Every entry has all four parts, written for a reader with zero project context — no term used that the earlier lessons flagged as assuming shared context.

stages.title: Specify the monitoring plan
stages.instructions: For at least one of the failure modes, specify a monitoring check built around expected activity or state, not the specific cause. Name the threshold (and how you'd calibrate it against real data, even if estimated), who gets the alert, and the escalation path if the first recipient doesn't respond.
stages.checkpoint: The check is symptom-based rather than cause-specific, with a named accountable recipient and a stated escalation path.

stages.title: Design the off switch and the operator training plan
stages.instructions: Specify what 'off' means concretely for this system, exactly how to trigger it, who is pre-authorized to use it, and what handles incoming work while it's off. Then describe, briefly, how you'd train the named operator — what real scenario they'd work through hands-on, and what would count as evidence the training worked.
stages.checkpoint: The off switch has a named, pre-authorized user and a documented temporary fallback, and the training plan uses a real scenario with an observable success criterion, not a demo.

rubric.criterion: The operator is correctly identified, not assumed to be the sponsor
rubric.meets: The write-up names a specific role or person as the day-to-day operator, with a stated reason distinguishing them from whoever commissioned the project.

rubric.criterion: Runbook entries are usable by a reader with zero project context
rubric.meets: Every entry names an observable symptom, an exact location, literal steps, and a named escalation contact — no term assumes the reader already has technical or project context.

rubric.criterion: Failure modes are specific to this system, not generic
rubric.meets: Each named failure mode is grounded in something this particular system actually depends on, not a boilerplate list.

rubric.criterion: The monitoring check is symptom-based, not cause-specific
rubric.meets: The check would catch multiple different underlying causes, and its threshold is justified against real or estimated normal behavior.

rubric.criterion: The off switch is genuinely usable without the consultant
rubric.meets: A specific, already-authorized person can trigger it and knows the immediate next step for incoming work, without needing anyone's real-time permission.

rubric.criterion: The training plan is scenario-based with an observable success criterion
rubric.meets: Training is built around a real runbook scenario worked through hands-on, with a stated way to tell whether it actually worked, not just whether it was delivered.

contentSections.body: A handover pack tested against a reader who wasn't in the room when the system was built is the only version of "they can run it without me" you're entitled to hand over.

title: Checkpoint — Building Something They Can Run Without You
description: Ten questions: four from this module, four from the previous module, two from three modules back. Ungraded, untimed, and getting one wrong just means it comes back later.

learningObjectives.text: Retrieve this module's handover distinctions, and earlier modules' integration and pipeline-design distinctions, without looking them up

contentSections.title: Checkpoint — Building Something They Can Run Without You

questions.from: This module — Building Something They Can Run Without You
questions.prompt: Corrigan & Vale's intake automation ran silently broken for eleven days after a vendor changed a webhook format. What was the actual root gap, per this module — not the vendor's change itself?

options.label: Nobody at Corrigan & Vale understood the automation well enough to know it existed as a discrete system, notice it had broken, or know who to call
The automation's code had a bug that caused the outage
The vendor should have been contractually required to give advance notice of format changes

questions.explanation: The vendor's change was a real, foreseeable kind of external event, not a design flaw — the actual failure was upstream of the code: nobody at the client had the understanding, monitoring, or ownership needed to detect and respond to it.

questions.from: This module — Building Something They Can Run Without You
questions.prompt: Why was "check the intake step's logs and restart the poller if stale" useless to Marisol, the pharmacy technician, even though it was accurate?

options.label: It assumed a reader who already knew what the logs were, where to find them, and what "the poller" referred to — context Marisol never had
The instruction was factually wrong about how to fix the problem
It was too short to be taken seriously

questions.explanation: The note was written for the person who built the system, not for a reader with zero shared context — a real runbook entry names the exact observable symptom, exact location, and literal steps, none of which this note provided.

questions.from: This module — Building Something They Can Run Without You
questions.prompt: Why did an hourly check for "has new intake appeared in the last two hours" catch the vendor's webhook format change without needing to specifically detect that change?

options.label: The check was built around expected activity, not around the specific cause — it catches any failure that produces the same symptom (no new activity), regardless of underlying cause
The check was specifically designed to detect webhook format changes
The check worked by coincidence and wouldn't reliably catch a different kind of failure

questions.explanation: Symptom-based monitoring — is expected activity happening — catches an entire category of causes without needing to predict each one individually, which is what made it effective against a failure mode nobody anticipated in advance.

questions.from: This module — Building Something They Can Run Without You
questions.prompt: Why did training Corrigan & Vale's owner, instead of the pharmacy technicians, fail to prepare anyone to actually run the system?

options.label: The owner was the sponsor, not the day-to-day operator — training aimed at whoever is in the kickoff and sales conversations misses the people who actually encounter the system every day
The owner wasn't technically capable of understanding the training material
The training session was too short to cover everything

questions.explanation: The sponsor and the day-to-day operator are often different people, and training defaults to whoever's in the room during sales and kickoff (usually the sponsor) unless the actual operators are deliberately identified and trained directly.

questions.from: Previous module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: Per the previous module, why did a consultant's architecture sketch assuming ScriptLedger had a live API turn out to be unusable?

options.label: It was designed around an assumption about the target system instead of a fact confirmed by whoever administers it — ScriptLedger actually had no API at all
The sketch was too detailed for the engagement's budget
APIs are generally an unreliable integration mechanism

questions.explanation: The existing systems set the actual boundary of what's buildable — the previous module's opening lesson was about confirming that boundary through discovery before designing anything, not assuming it from how comparable systems usually work.

questions.from: Previous module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: Why was ScriptLedger's nightly export a poor fit for the same-day double-dispense check?

options.label: The export was always at least a day stale, and the check needed to know about something filled earlier the same day — a need the export structurally couldn't satisfy
The export file format was incompatible with the intake tool
Nightly exports should never be relied on for any purpose

questions.explanation: The right integration tier depends on matching staleness tolerance to the task's actual requirement — a same-day check has zero tolerance for a day of staleness, unlike the weekly report or trend dashboard the same export served fine.

questions.from: Previous module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: Why did a shared "svc-automation" login with full pharmacist permissions fail the pharmacy board's audit requirement?

options.label: Every action needed to trace to a specific licensed individual, and a shared login with broad permissions made actions untraceable to what actually caused them
Shared logins are technically incompatible with ScriptLedger's software
The board prohibits any automated action on dispensing records under any identity

questions.explanation: The board's requirement was about individual accountability specifically — a distinct, narrowly-scoped service identity is what makes automated actions traceable and contains what a bug in the automation could actually do.

questions.from: Previous module — Integration and the Systems Already There
questions.prompt: Why did the write-back step of queuing a refill request deserve more design scrutiny than the earlier read-only extraction stages?

options.label: A mistake at the write-back stage becomes a real, actionable order, while a mistake at a read stage produces a wrong report a human still has a chance to catch before anything real happens
The write-back stage was more technically difficult to implement
Write-back stages are always slower to execute than read stages

questions.explanation: The module's distinction was about consequence, not difficulty — a write-back stage changes the system of record itself, which is why it needs validation before the write, a genuinely unconfirmed state, and a rollback path that read-only stages don't.

questions.from: Three modules back — Designing the Pipeline
questions.prompt: Per the pipeline-design module, what was actually missing when two Fennimore engineers each built a working step, but one output a field called "rate" while the next expected "totalRate"?

options.label: A step contract — a written specification of exactly what one step guarantees and what the next requires, so the handoff isn't assumed
More thorough testing of each step individually
A faster model for the extraction step

questions.explanation: Both steps worked correctly in isolation — the actual gap was an unwritten handoff contract between them, the same category of problem this module's runbook lesson addresses at the human-handoff level instead of the code level.

questions.from: Three modules back — Designing the Pipeline
questions.prompt: Why did Fennimore's overnight batch job produce 40 duplicate bookings after crashing and automatically restarting partway through?

options.label: The job lacked idempotency — nothing made re-running the same batch safe, so the restart redid work it had already completed
The batch size was too large for the server to handle
The network connection was too unreliable for an overnight job

questions.explanation: A crash-and-restart is expected for an unattended job; the real gap was that re-running wasn't safe, because nothing let the job recognize which items it had already processed.

contentSections.body: Anything that didn't come back will return in a later checkpoint. That's the design, not a failure.
